items.title: Skills as Sub-Agents: Orchestrating Complex work with Claude Skills
items.summary:
If you've built anything with a coding agent, you've hit the wall: the task is too big for one prompt. You ask it to "find out what's causing this bug," and it starts strong — then drowns. Half its context is the raw output of files it dumped, it's lost the thread of which theory it was testing, and the answer it finally gives is confidently wrong. The problem isn't the model. It's that you asked one agent, with one context window, to do everything — gather evidence, hold it all in its head, and reason about it at the same time. There's a cleaner pattern. Split the work into skills , and have one skill orchestrate the others as sub-agents . Let's walk through it. New to skills or the agent loop? The one-line version: a skill is a packaged set of instructions on disk that the agent loads only when it's relevant. A sub-agent is a fresh agent instance with its own separate context window. This post is about combining the two. The core idea: reasoning up top, work down below Picture two layers. The orchestrator sits on top. Its only job is to think : plan the investigation, interpret results, decide what to do next, and conclude. It never opens a file, never greps the codebase, never parses output. The first lines of an orchestrator skill should say exactly that: You are a reasoning and coordination layer. You think, you plan, you interpret, you propose — but you never dig into the data yourself. That work belongs in sub-agents. The workers sit below. Each is a small, focused skill that does one concrete thing — find every usage of a function, read a file's git history, run a specific test. The orchestrator spawns each worker as a sub-agent : a separate agent with its own fresh context window. Why does this split matter so much? Context hygiene. When a worker greps a huge codebase and reads a dozen files, all of that lands in the worker's context — not the orchestrator's. The worker chews through it, extracts the one thing that matters, and reports back a three-line summary. The orchestrator's context stays clean: it accumulates conclusions , not raw data . That's the whole trick, and it's why the orchestrator can run for dozens of steps without falling over. Anatomy of a worker skill A worker skill is just a folder with a SKILL.md file. The front matter does the heavy lifting: --- name : find-usages description : " Find every place a symbol, function, or pattern is used across the codebase. Use when tracing how a change ripples through the code." context : fork allowed-tools : Grep, Read argument-hint : [--path= ] --- # Find Usages ## Input - **Symbol** (required): the function, class, or pattern to trace. - **Path** (optional): limit the search to a directory. - **Output file** : write your full report here. ## Procedure 1. Search the codebase for the symbol. 2. For each hit, read enough surrounding code to classify it
   (definition, call site, test, re-export). 3. Write the full annotated list to the output file. 4. Return a 3-line summary: total count, and the 1–2 most relevant sites. Four things are worth calling out, because they're what make it composable: description — this is the skill's résumé. It's how the orchestrator decides whether to call this worker at all (more on that below). Write it for selection , not just documentation. context: fork — run this skill in an isolated context. This is what makes it a sub-agent instead of inline instructions. allowed-tools — scope the worker down to only what it needs. A read-only search worker gets Grep, Read and nothing that can modify files. This is your safety boundary, enforced per-skill. The output contract — the worker writes its full findings to a file and returns only a summary . This is the single most important convention in the whole system. Get it right and everything else falls into place. The summary-vs-report split Say it plainly, because it's the load-bearing idea: A sub-agent writes its full report to a file , and returns only a short summary to the orchestrator. The orchestrator reads the summary immediately. If it needs the details — the exact line, the full list — it reads the file on demand . Most of the time it doesn't need to. So the expensive raw data lives on disk, referenced by path, instead of clogging the reasoning layer's context. How the orchestrator picks workers (without reading them all) Here's a subtlety that trips people up. If the orchestrator has twenty worker skills available, you might think it needs to read all twenty SKILL.md files to know what they do. That would blow its context before the work even starts. It doesn't. The agent already sees every skill's name and one-line description — that's the progressive-disclosure model skills are built on. So the orchestrator picks workers by description alone . Make this an explicit rule in the orchestrator: Do NOT read the full worker SKILL.md files — they are large and will pollute your context. The skill name and description are enough to pick. This is why that description field is so important. It's not documentation for humans; it's the interface the orchestrator selects against. The orchestration loop Put it together and the orchestrator runs a loop that should feel familiar if you've seen the basic agent loop — just one level up. Underneath any specific task it's the same four beats: PLAN (once)
  Confirm the request, scope it, restate the goal.
repeat:
  DISPATCH    → spawn worker sub-agents in parallel to do the next chunk
  INTEGRATE   → read each summary as it returns, update your working picture
  DECIDE      → goal met? finish. gaps remain? dispatch more.
DELIVER
  Present the result (with alternatives called out if you're unsure) and stop. That's the general shape. Each kind of task just fills in the blanks differently: Task type DISPATCH gathers… The "working picture" is… DELIVER produces… Debugging evidence about a failure competing hypotheses root cause + fix Research facts from sources an outline of the answer a synthesized report Migration which files need changing a checklist of edits a completed, verified change Audit findings per rule/area a running list of issues a prioritized report The vocabulary changes; the loop doesn't. Whenever a task is "break it into independent chunks, do them, combine the results, repeat until done," this is the pattern. A few things make it work well in practice: Fan out, then integrate as results arrive. The orchestrator spawns workers as background sub-agents and doesn't block waiting for all of them. As each summary comes back, it folds it into the picture and — crucially — can dispatch a follow-up immediately. A usage search turns up a suspicious call site? Fire off a git-history worker on that file now , while the other workers are still running. The loop is interleaved, not batch-then-wait. Cap the expensive workers. Cheap, read-only workers (a quick search, a file read) have no concurrency limit — the cost of running one you didn't need is near zero. Heavier workers (running the full test suite, deep analysis) get a hard cap, e.g. "at most 2 at a time." Match the limit to the cost. Refresh the instructions each phase. On a long run, the orchestrator's own SKILL.md scrolls out of its context. So each phase's detailed rules live in a separate file ( phase-collect.md , phase-synthesize.md …) that the orchestrator re-reads every time it enters that phase . Don't rely on the agent remembering a rule it read forty steps ago — put the rule back in front of it when it's about to act on it. Keep an append-only log. One file is the run's source of truth: every dispatch, every result, every decision. Append-only — if an earlier note was wrong, you add a correction rather than editing history. It's the audit trail and the memory that survives context churn. Why this beats one big prompt Context stays clean. Raw data is quarantined in worker contexts. The reasoning layer only ever sees distilled conclusions, so it can go deep and long without degrading. Real parallelism. Ten independent checks run at once instead of one after another. A job that would take an agent twenty sequential steps finishes in a handful of rounds. Specialization. Each worker is small, testable, and good at exactly one thing. You can improve the usage-finder without touching anything else. Safety per worker. allowed-tools means your read-only workers cannot modify files, no matter what the model decides. The boundary is structural, not a polite request in a prompt. Composability. Adding a capability means adding a skill folder. The orchestrator picks it up by description — no changes to the loop. Setting up your own The pattern transfers to any complex task — debugging, research, migrations, audits. A starting recipe: Write the workers first. For each concrete sub-task, make a skill folder with a SKILL.md . Nail the description (for selection), set context: fork , scope allowed-tools , and define the input params + output-file contract. Enforce summary-vs-report everywhere. Every worker writes full output to a file, returns a short summary. Non-negotiable — it's what keeps the orchestrator's context alive. Write the orchestrator as pure reasoning. Tell it, in the strongest terms, to delegate all the actual work. Give it a loop (gather → interpret → decide) and the rule to pick workers by description, not by reading them. Externalize per-phase rules. Put detailed checklists in phase files the orchestrator re-reads on entry, so they stay in its attention on long runs. Cap the expensive workers and log everything. Concurrency limits by cost; an append-only log as the source of truth.
That's the architecture. One agent that thinks, many that fetch — each in its own context, each doing one job well. Once you stop cramming everything into a single prompt and start treating skills as sub-agents, the ceiling on what an agent can reliably handle goes way, way up.

Anatomy of a worker skill

A worker skill is just a folder with a SKILL.md file. The front matter does the heavy lifting:

---
name: find-usages
description: "Find every place a symbol, function, or pattern is used across the codebase. Use when tracing how a change ripples through the code."
context: fork
allowed-tools: Grep, Read
argument-hint:  [--path=]
---
# Find Usages
## Input
- **Symbol** (required): the function, class, or pattern to trace.
- **Path** (optional): limit the search to a directory.
- **Output file**: write your full report here.
## Procedure
1. Search the codebase for the symbol.
2. For each hit, read enough surrounding code to classify it
   (definition, call site, test, re-export).
3. Write the full annotated list to the output file.
4. Return a 3-line summary: total count, and the 1–2 most relevant sites.

  • description — this is the skill's résumé. It's how the orchestrator decides whether to call this worker at all (more on that below). Write it for selection, not just documentation.
  • context: fork — run this skill in an isolated context. This is what makes it a sub-agent instead of inline instructions.
  • allowed-tools — scope the worker down to only what it needs. A read-only search worker gets Grep, Read and nothing that can modify files. This is your safety boundary, enforced per-skill.
  • The output contract — the worker writes its full findings to a file and returns only a summary. This is the single most important convention in the whole system. Get it right and everything else falls into place.
The summary-vs-report split

Say it plainly, because it's the load-bearing idea:

A sub-agent writes its full report to a file, and returns only a short summary to the orchestrator.

The orchestrator reads the summary immediately. If it needs the details — the exact line, the full list — it reads the file on demand. Most of the time it doesn't need to. So the expensive raw data lives on disk, referenced by path, instead of clogging the reasoning layer's context.

It doesn't. The agent already sees every skill's name and one-line description — that's the progressive-disclosure model skills are built on. So the orchestrator picks workers by description alone. Make this an explicit rule in the orchestrator:

Do NOT read the full worker SKILL.md files — they are large and will pollute your context. The skill name and description are enough to pick.
This is why that description field is so important. It's not documentation for humans; it's the interface the orchestrator selects against.

The orchestration loop

Put it together and the orchestrator runs a loop that should feel familiar if you've seen the basic agent loop — just one level up. Underneath any specific task it's the same four beats:

PLAN (once)
  Confirm the request, scope it, restate the goal.
repeat:
  DISPATCH    → spawn worker sub-agents in parallel to do the next chunk
  INTEGRATE   → read each summary as it returns, update your working picture
  DECIDE      → goal met? finish. gaps remain? dispatch more.
DELIVER
  Present the result (with alternatives called out if you're unsure) and stop.

That's the general shape. Each kind of task just fills in the blanks differently:

Task type DISPATCH gathers… The "working picture" is… DELIVER produces… Debugging evidence about a failure competing hypotheses root cause + fix Research facts from sources an outline of the answer a synthesized report Migration which files need changing a checklist of edits a completed, verified change Audit findings per rule/area a running list of issues a prioritized report

The vocabulary changes; the loop doesn't. Whenever a task is "break it into independent chunks, do them, combine the results, repeat until done," this is the pattern.
A few things make it work well in practice:
Fan out, then integrate as results arrive. The orchestrator spawns workers as background sub-agents and doesn't block waiting for all of them. As each summary comes back, it folds it into the picture and — crucially — can dispatch a follow-up immediately. A usage search turns up a suspicious call site? Refresh the instructions each phase. On a long run, the orchestrator's own SKILL.md scrolls out of its context. So each phase's detailed rules live in a separate file (phase-collect.md, phase-synthesize.md…) that the orchestrator re-reads every time it enters that phase. Don't rely on the agent remembering a rule it read forty steps ago — put the rule back in front of it when it's about to act on it.
Keep an append-only log. One file is the run's source of truth: every dispatch, every result, every decision. Append-only — if an earlier note was wrong, you add a correction rather than editing history. It's the audit trail and the memory that survives context churn.

Why this beats one big prompt
  • Context stays clean. Raw data is quarantined in worker contexts. The reasoning layer only ever sees distilled conclusions, so it can go deep and long without degrading.
  • Real parallelism. Ten independent checks run at once instead of one after another. A job that would take an agent twenty sequential steps finishes in a handful of rounds.
  • Specialization. Each worker is small, testable, and good at exactly one thing. You can improve the usage-finder without touching anything else.
  • Safety per worker. allowed-tools means your read-only workers cannot modify files, no matter what the model decides. The boundary is structural, not a polite request in a prompt.
  • Composability. Adding a capability means adding a skill folder. The orchestrator picks it up by description — no changes to the loop.
Setting up your own

The pattern transfers to any complex task — debugging, research, migrations, audits. A starting recipe:

  1. Write the workers first. For each concrete sub-task, make a skill folder with a SKILL.md. Nail the description (for selection), set context: fork, scope allowed-tools, and define the input params + output-file contract.
  2. Enforce summary-vs-report everywhere. Every worker writes full output to a file, returns a short summary. Non-negotiable — it's what keeps the orchestrator's context alive.
  3. Write the orchestrator as pure reasoning. Tell it, in the strongest terms, to delegate all the actual work. Give it a loop (gather → interpret → decide) and the rule to pick workers by description, not by reading them.
  4. Externalize per-phase rules. Put detailed checklists in phase files the orchestrator re-reads on entry, so they stay in its attention on long runs.
  5. Cap the expensive workers and log everything. Concurrency limits by cost; an append-only log as the source of truth. That's the architecture. One agent that thinks, many that fetch — each in its own context, each doing one job well. Once you stop cramming everything into a single prompt and start treating skills as sub-agents, the ceiling on what an agent can reliably handle goes way, way up.

items.title: Microsoft Foundry as the Master Cloud, Google ADK as the Client: Cross-Cloud A2A v1.0
items.summary:
This installment puts Microsoft Foundry in charge . Azure is the main cloud: it hosts the master agent, owns the exchange-rate tool, and does all of the arithmetic. Google Cloud gets the junior role — an ADK client on Cloud Run whose entire job is to authenticate, discover, and delegate over A2A v1.0. That is a real architecture rather than a demo curiosity. If your organization's governance, models, and data already live in Azure, you do not want the Google side owning orchestration; you want it as a reachable client that can be pointed at a master it does not control. The previous article in this series set the roles the other way around and measured the hop. This one is about what changes when Foundry is the one being called — and almost everything that changed was authentication and discovery, not protocol. It is deployed and measured: Cloud Run in us-central1 calling a Foundry master in eastus2 , live rates, numbers at the end. Four things broke on the way, all of them invisible to a green test suite, and those are the interesting part. Where the Work Lives Google Cloud Run
Google ADK client (RemoteA2aAgent)
      |
      +-- A2A v1.0 / JSON-RPC + Microsoft Entra
             |
             v
Microsoft Foundry hosted master (Microsoft Agent Framework)
      |
      +-- MCP stdio --> Frankfurter exchange rates The important design decision: the tool travels with the master. Foundry owns the MCP rate tool and all the Decimal arithmetic; the ADK side is a thin authenticated proxy that owns the client session and nothing else. That is what makes Azure the main cloud in a meaningful sense rather than a decorative one — capability lives there, and the Google side cannot answer a currency question on its own even if it wanted to. It also keeps the experiment honest. If you make Foundry the master but leave the tool on the ADK side, you have not tested a cross-cloud master at all — you have tested your own MCP server twice with extra latency in the middle. The two role assignments live in separate directories ( foundry_master/ and google_adk_client/ , versus the earlier coordinator/ and adk_agent/ ) so neither can quietly become the other's dependency, and nothing calls anything recursively. Part One: A Foundry Agent That Answers the Phone The master is an ordinary Agent Framework agent. The only thing that marks it as a hosted agent is ResponsesHostServer : from agent_framework import Agent , MCPStdioTool from agent_framework.foundry import FoundryChatClient from agent_framework_foundry_hosting import ResponsesHostServer def build_agent () -> Agent : client = FoundryChatClient ( project_endpoint = os . environ [ " FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT " ], model = os . environ [ " AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME " ], credential = DefaultAzureCredential (), ) return Agent ( client = client , name = " currency-master-agent " , description = " Master currency agent called remotely by Google ADK. " , instructions = INSTRUCTIONS , tools = [ build_rate_tool ()], default_options = { " store " : False }, ) ResponsesHostServer ( build_agent ()). run () The instructions are deliberately joyless, because the master is the side doing the arithmetic and I do not want a language model anywhere near it: For every conversion, call convert_currency once for each requested target. Copy the tool's decimal strings exactly and never perform or verify arithmetic yourself. Reply with exactly one JSON object per target and no other text. The rate tool is an MCP stdio subprocess, spawned inside the hosted container: MCPStdioTool ( name = " currency_rates " , command = sys . executable , args = [ " -m " , " mcp_server.server " ], env = { " PYTHONPATH " : os . getenv ( " PYTHONPATH " , os . getcwd ()), ...}, load_prompts = False , ) That -m mcp_server.server is where the first non-obvious problem lives. The hosted deploy bundle is the foundry_master/ directory, not the repository root, so the MCP subprocess cannot import mcp_server/ and coordinator/ — the code is simply not in the image. The deploy helper synchronizes them in before handing the directory to azd : rsync -a --delete " $REPO_ROOT /coordinator/" " $MASTER_DIR /coordinator/" rsync -a --delete " $REPO_ROOT /mcp_server/" " $MASTER_DIR /mcp_server/" cd " $MASTER_DIR " && azd provision && azd deploy Not elegant. But an MCP stdio tool means a real subprocess with a real import path, and hosted runtimes do not care about your monorepo layout. The azure.yaml declares the model deployment and the hosting protocol together, which is a nice property of the Foundry azd provider — one file provisions gpt-5-mini and the agent that uses it: services : currency-master-agent : host : azure.ai.agent codeConfiguration : dependencyResolution : remote_build entryPoint : main.py runtime : python_3_13 protocols : - protocol : responses version : 2.0.0 Note what that protocols list says: responses . Not A2A. Part Two: Incoming A2A Is Opt-In, and It Is Preview A hosted Foundry agent speaks the Responses protocol. It does not speak A2A to inbound callers until you explicitly turn that on, and at the time of writing that is a preview capability with no azd surface. It is a PATCH against the agent, and the two things it must get right are: { " agent_card " : { " description " : " Master currency agent using live MCP rates and Decimal arithmetic. " , " version " : " 1.0 " , " skills " : [{ " id " : " currency-conversion " , " name " : " Currency conversion " , ...}], }, " agent_endpoint " : { " protocol_configuration " : { " responses " : {}, " a2a " : {}}}, } First, you supply the agent card yourself. Coming from ADK — where to_a2a() derives a card from the agent, and MCP tools show up as skills automatically — writing the card by hand feels like a step backwards. It is also a step towards honesty: the card is a contract, and on this side you are made to state it. Second, the patch sends both protocols, never just a2a . That turns out to matter, and rather than assume, I probed it against the deployed agent — patch with a2a alone, read the state back, then restore: before:            protocols ['a2a', 'responses']   card 200
patch a2a-only ->  200
after a2a-only:    protocols ['a2a']                card 400
patch both ->      200
after restore:     protocols ['a2a', 'responses']   card 200 So protocol_configuration replaces; it does not merge. Send {"a2a": {}} on its own and Responses is gone from a running agent. The second column is the part I did not expect: with Responses removed, the A2A agent card itself started returning 400 . The A2A surface is not independent of the Responses protocol — knocking out Responses took A2A down with it. So the failure mode of "just enable the protocol I want" is not "Responses breaks," it is "everything breaks," and the request that did it returns a cheerful 200 . A unit test pins the shape so nobody trims it back later: def test_patch_retains_responses_when_enabling_a2a (): protocols = patch_body ()[ " agent_endpoint " ][ " protocol_configuration " ] assert set ( protocols ) == { " responses " , " a2a " } One more trap while reading state back: definition.protocol_versions still reports only responses on a working A2A agent. That field describes what the container speaks. Enablement lives in agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration . I checked the wrong field first and briefly concluded the patch had done nothing. Part Three: Even the Agent Card Needs a Token In the Azure-calls-Google direction, discovery is anonymous. You GET a URL, you get JSON, you read the skills. The card is public metadata. Calling into Foundry, there is no anonymous /.well-known/agent-card.json . The card lives at a versioned path under the agent's protocol endpoint: {project_endpoint}/agents/currency-master-agent/endpoint/protocols/a2a/agentCard/v1.0 and every request to it — the card fetch included — carries an Entra bearer token. The caller's identity needs the Foundry Agent Consumer role on the Foundry project . That is a data-plane role assignment, separate from any control-plane rights the same principal might already have. The practical consequence to expect: a 404 or 401 on the card is as likely to be a missing role assignment as a wrong URL, so check Access Control before you start counting path segments. Discovery being authenticated also changes the trust story in a way worth stating plainly. When ADK is the one being called, anyone can read what that agent claims to do. With Foundry as the master, capability discovery is itself a privileged operation — you cannot enumerate the master's skills without already being allowed to call it. For a main cloud that owns the tools, that is arguably the correct default. Part Four: The Google Side Needs a Credential That Isn't Google's This is the part with no counterpart when Google hosts the master. A Cloud Run container authenticating to Azure needs an Entra service principal, which means a client secret has to exist somewhere on the Google side. It goes in Secret Manager and is injected at deploy time — never in source, never in a manifest: gcloud run deploy " $SERVICE " \ --source " $REPO_ROOT /google_adk_client" \ --no-allow-unauthenticated \ --set-secrets "AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET= ${ AZURE_SECRET } :latest" \ --set-env-vars "FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT= ${ FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT } ,AZURE_TENANT_ID=...,AZURE_CLIENT_ID=..." The deploy helper refuses to take a raw secret value at all — it asserts the secret already exists ( gcloud secrets describe ) and fails if it does not. Convenience flags that accept secret values are how secrets end up in shell history. DefaultAzureCredential then picks up tenant, client ID, and secret from the environment. Attaching the token to outbound A2A traffic is a small httpx.Auth adapter — cached, refreshed five minutes before expiry, and stamping the protocol version on every request: class EntraAuth ( httpx . Auth ): requires_request_body = True async def async_auth_flow ( self , request ): if self . _token is None or self . _token . expires_on - 300 <= time . time (): self . _token = await self . _credential . get_token ( " https://ai.azure.com/.default " ) request . headers [ " Authorization " ] = f " Bearer { self . _token . token } " request . headers [ " A2A-Version " ] = " 1.0 " yield request The scope is https://ai.azure.com/.default — the AI services audience, not the ARM audience. A token for the wrong audience is a perfectly valid token that gets rejected, which produces a 401 that looks nothing like a scope problem. And that is the entire Google side of the integration: def build_root_agent () -> RemoteA2aAgent : client = httpx . AsyncClient ( auth = EntraAuth (), timeout = httpx . Timeout ( 120 )) return RemoteA2aAgent ( name = " foundry_currency_master " , description = " Authenticated ADK proxy to the Azure Foundry currency master. " , agent_card = agent_card_url ( os . environ [ " FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT " ]), httpx_client = client , timeout = 120 , full_history_when_stateless = False , ) RemoteA2aAgent accepting an injected httpx_client is what makes this possible without patching ADK. Everything unusual about this integration — Entra tokens, a non-standard card path, a 120-second cross-cloud timeout — fits in the client you hand it. That is a genuinely good extension point, and it is the reason "ADK calls Azure" is thirty lines instead of a fork. Two smaller choices worth flagging: full_history_when_stateless=False keeps the proxy from re-sending accumulated conversation on every hop, and the 120-second timeout is the same lesson from the previous article, learned again — a default tuned for one cloud is not a default for two. Cold start plus model generation plus a live rate call crosses ten seconds without trying. A Packaging Bug That No Unit Test Can See Two bugs in the client image, both found by reconstructing the container's directory layout locally and running ADK's AgentLoader against it — not by watching it fail in Cloud Run. The image runs adk api_server /app , and /app holds agent.py next to entra_auth.py . ADK 2.5.0 detects that as single-agent mode : it takes the directory's parent as the agents directory and imports your file as app.agent . Your agent module is therefore a submodule of a package , not a top-level script. Which means this, in agent.py , cannot work: from entra_auth import EntraAuth # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'entra_auth' and this can: from .entra_auth import EntraAuth The loader puts / on sys.path , not /app , so the flat import has nowhere to resolve from. The relative import works in both contexts — inside the container and when the repo's unit tests import the same module as google_adk_client.entra_auth . The other half of the same mistake: a COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock agent.py ./ line that never mentions entra_auth.py , so the module is not in the image at all. Nothing fails at build time — the import is what fails. Both are invisible to a green test suite, because the tests import google_adk_client.entra_auth from the source tree, and the source tree is not what ships. Loading the reconstructed /app layout is a two-line check that catches both: from google.adk.cli.utils.agent_loader import AgentLoader AgentLoader ( " /app " ). load_agent ( " app " ) # ModuleNotFoundError before the fix Deploying It Order matters, because the ADK client needs an endpoint that does not exist until the master is up and A2A is enabled on it: ./infra/deploy_foundry_master.sh # provision, deploy, then PATCH incoming A2A on export FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT = "https://.../endpoint/protocols/a2a" export GCP_PROJECT = "your-project" AZURE_TENANT_ID = "..." AZURE_CLIENT_ID = "..." ./infra/deploy_google_adk_client.sh # ADK proxy on Cloud Run, secret from Secret Manager The enable script prints the resolved card and the endpoint to export, so the second step is a copy-paste rather than a URL you assemble by hand. Two Things That Only Broke When It Ran The unit tests were green the whole time. Neither of these was visible to them. The v1.0 method name is not the v0.3 method name. A hand-written JSON-RPC call using message/send — the v0.3 spelling that most A2A examples still show — comes back as: { "error" : { "code" : -32601 , "message" : "Method not found" , "data" : [{ "reason" : "METHOD_NOT_FOUND" , "metadata" : { "detail" : "'method' field is not a valid A2A method." }}]}} In a2a-sdk 1.x the JSON-RPC method is SendMessage , with proto-JSON params. Worth knowing that the Foundry card advertises three interfaces on the same URL — JSONRPC 1.0, JSONRPC 0.3, and HTTP+JSON 0.3 — so the server is not the thing constraining you; your client's spelling is. The container needed a dependency nothing declared. azure.identity.aio builds its async transport with aiohttp , which is not a hard dependency of azure-identity . It is present on a normal workstation, so local runs pass. In a uv sync --frozen container it is absent, the build succeeds, and the first token request dies: File "azure/core/pipeline/transport/__init__.py", line 94, in __getattr__
    raise ImportError("aiohttp package is not installed") Both bugs share a shape: the lockfile and the source tree that tests run against are not the artifact that ships. Results All figures below are from the live deployment — Cloud Run in us-central1 calling a Foundry master in eastus2 , gpt-5-mini, live Frankfurter rates, the prompt Convert 250 GBP to USD and JPY. Measurement Value Authenticated agent-card GET (warm median, 6 runs) 0.35 s Same, first fetch 0.51 s A2A SendMessage , workstation → master (warm median, 6 runs) 21.2 s A2A round trip via the Cloud Run ADK client (median, 5 runs) 23.4 s Same, range 18.9 s – 29.5 s First request against a fresh Cloud Run revision 20.8 s Every run returned the same numbers, and they are the right ones: { "source_currency" : "GBP" , "target_currency" : "USD" , "rate" : "1.3389" , "converted_amount" : "334.7250" , "source" : "frankfurter-live" } { "source_currency" : "GBP" , "target_currency" : "JPY" , "rate" : "218.15" , "converted_amount" : "54537.50" , "source" : "frankfurter-live" } Three things stand out. Authenticated discovery is cheap. The worry going in was that a card fetch requiring a token and a role check would be meaningfully more expensive than an anonymous GET . At 0.35 s warm it is noise next to the call it precedes, and the token is cached across calls anyway. The ADK proxy hop costs about 2 seconds — 21.2 s direct versus 23.4 s through Cloud Run, against a spread of 18.9–29.5 s. Put plainly, the run-to-run variance of the master is larger than the entire cost of putting a second cloud in the path. The master dominates everything. Roughly 20 seconds of a 23-second round trip is gpt-5-mini deciding to call convert_currency twice and waiting on Frankfurter each time. If you want this architecture faster, the protocol and the proxy are not where the time is. Note the contrast with the previous article's Azure-orchestrating-Google numbers ( a2a_only at 1.69 s median): same protocol, same clouds, an order of magnitude apart — because there the remote agent answered one question, and here the master runs a multi-tool reasoning loop. Protocol overhead is not what you are measuring in either case. Infrastructure timings, for anyone budgeting a first deploy: azd provision 64 s, azd deploy 116 s, and — the one that will confuse you — 105 seconds before data-plane RBAC took effect. Agent writes kept returning 403 with the role assignment already visible in az role assignment list . It is propagation, not misconfiguration. Wait it out before you start re-assigning roles. Raw results are in evaluations/results/foundry-master-live-2026-07-31.json , and evaluations/measure_foundry_master.py regenerates them. One caveat on scope: these are single-prompt samples, not a distribution. The 38-case evaluation matrix from the previous article has not been re-run against this architecture yet. Lessons Making Foundry the master is an auth problem, not a protocol problem. The
JSON-RPC half is the easy half whichever cloud is in charge. Budget your time
for identity — and for RBAC propagation, which took 105 seconds here while
the assignment already showed as present. Discovery is not always free — but it is cheap. An authenticated agent
card makes every "card not found" a role assignment until proven otherwise.
It costs 0.35 s warm, which is not the thing to optimize. protocol_configuration replaces, it does not merge. Verified, not
assumed: patching a2a alone dropped Responses and took the A2A card down
with it (400), and the request that did it returned 200. Send every protocol
you want to keep, and pin it with a test. Hosted runtimes flatten your repo layout. An MCP stdio tool spawns a real
subprocess with a real import path — if your deploy bundle is a
subdirectory, the imports have to be inside it. Cross-cloud credentials live on the calling side. Google calling Azure
means an Azure client secret in Google Secret Manager. There is no way around
the secret; there is a way around having it in your source tree. Get the token audience right before you debug anything else. A valid
token for the wrong scope fails in a way that looks like a permissions bug. Injectable HTTP clients are what make cross-vendor agents cheap. ADK's RemoteA2aAgent taking an httpx_client is the difference between an
adapter and a fork. Your tests import the source tree; your users run the image. A missing COPY line, a flat import that only works outside a package, and a
transitive dependency your workstation happens to have ( aiohttp ) were all
invisible to a green test suite. Load the container's real layout, or deploy
and call it — those are the only two things that find this class of bug. Check the method name before you check your permissions. message/send is v0.3; SendMessage is v1.x. The failure is METHOD_NOT_FOUND on an
endpoint you are fully authorized to call. The protocol is never the slow part. ~20 s of a 23 s round trip was the
master's own reasoning and tool calls. The second cloud cost about 2 s —
less than the master's run-to-run variance. Source Both role assignments, the deploy scripts, and the tests: GitHub - xbill9/foundry-adk-a2a-currency The Foundry-as-master components are foundry_master/ , google_adk_client/ , and infra/enable_foundry_master_a2a.py . Measurements come from evaluations/measure_foundry_master.py , raw output in evaluations/results/foundry-master-live-2026-07-31.json . The setup where Google hosts the remote agent, along with its benchmark results, is in the previous article in this series. If you have run incoming A2A on a hosted Foundry agent — especially if your numbers differ, or you found a preview quirk this missed — I would like to compare notes.

from agent_framework import Agent, MCPStdioTool

def build_agent() -> Agent:
    client = FoundryChatClient(
        project_endpoint=os.environ["FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"],
        model=os.environ["AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME"],
        credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),

    codeConfiguration:

      entryPoint: main.py
      runtime: python_3_13
    protocols:
      - protocol: responses

Part Three: Even the Agent Card Needs a Token

In the Azure-calls-Google direction, discovery is anonymous. You GET a URL,
you get JSON, you read the skills. The card is public metadata.

Calling into Foundry, there is no anonymous /.well-known/agent-card.json. The
card lives at a versioned path under the agent's protocol endpoint:

{project_endpoint}/agents/currency-master-agent/endpoint/protocols/a2a/agentCard/v1.0

and every request to it — the card fetch included — carries an Entra bearer
token. The caller's identity needs the Foundry Agent Consumer role on the
Foundry project. That is a data-plane role assignment, separate from any
control-plane rights the same principal might already have.

The practical consequence to expect: a 404 or 401 on the card is as likely to be
a missing role assignment as a wrong URL, so check Access Control before you
start counting path segments.

Discovery being authenticated also changes the trust story in a way worth
stating plainly. When ADK is the one being called, anyone can read what that
agent claims to do. With Foundry as the master, capability discovery is itself a
privileged operation — you cannot enumerate the master's skills without already
being allowed to call it. For a main cloud that owns the tools, that is arguably
the correct default.

Part Four: The Google Side Needs a Credential That Isn't Google's

This is the part with no counterpart when Google hosts the master. A Cloud Run
container authenticating to Azure needs an Entra service principal, which means
a client secret has to exist somewhere on the Google side. It goes in Secret
Manager and is injected at deploy time — never in source, never in a manifest:

gcloud run deploy "$SERVICE" \
  --source "$REPO_ROOT/google_adk_client" \
  --no-allow-unauthenticated \
  --set-secrets "AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET=${AZURE_SECRET}:latest" \
  --set-env-vars "FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT=${FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT},AZURE_TENANT_ID=...,AZURE_CLIENT_ID=..."

The deploy helper refuses to take a raw secret value at all — it asserts the
secret already exists (gcloud secrets describe) and fails if it does not.
Convenience flags that accept secret values are how secrets end up in shell
history.

DefaultAzureCredential then picks up tenant, client ID, and secret from the
environment. Attaching the token to outbound A2A traffic is a small
httpx.Auth adapter — cached, refreshed five minutes before expiry, and
stamping the protocol version on every request:

class EntraAuth(httpx.Auth):
    requires_request_body = True

    async def async_auth_flow(self, request):
        if self._token is None or self._token.expires_on - 300 <= time.time():
            self._token = await self._credential.get_token("https://ai.azure.com/.default")
        request.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self._token.token}"
        request.headers["A2A-Version"] = "1.0"
        yield request

The scope is https://ai.azure.com/.default — the AI services audience, not the
ARM audience. A token for the wrong audience is a perfectly valid token that
gets rejected, which produces a 401 that looks nothing like a scope problem.

And that is the entire Google side of the integration:

def build_root_agent() -> RemoteA2aAgent:
    client = httpx.AsyncClient(auth=EntraAuth(), timeout=httpx.Timeout(120))
    return RemoteA2aAgent(
        name="foundry_currency_master",
        description="Authenticated ADK proxy to the Azure Foundry currency master.",
        agent_card=agent_card_url(os.environ["FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT"]),
        httpx_client=client,
        timeout=120,
        full_history_when_stateless=False,
    )

RemoteA2aAgent accepting an injected httpx_client is what makes this
possible without patching ADK. Everything unusual about this integration —
Entra tokens, a non-standard card path, a 120-second cross-cloud timeout — fits
in the client you hand it. That is a genuinely good extension point, and it is
the reason "ADK calls Azure" is thirty lines instead of a fork.

Two smaller choices worth flagging: full_history_when_stateless=False keeps the
proxy from re-sending accumulated conversation on every hop, and the 120-second
timeout is the same lesson from the previous article, learned again — a default
tuned for one cloud is not a default for two. Cold start plus model generation
plus a live rate call crosses ten seconds without trying.

A Packaging Bug That No Unit Test Can See

Two bugs in the client image, both found by reconstructing the container's
directory layout locally and running ADK's AgentLoader against it — not by
watching it fail in Cloud Run.

The image runs adk api_server /app, and /app holds agent.py next to
entra_auth.py. ADK 2.5.0 detects that as single-agent mode: it takes the
directory's parent as the agents directory and imports your file as app.agent.
Your agent module is therefore a submodule of a package, not a top-level
script.

Which means this, in agent.py, cannot work:

from entra_auth import EntraAuth      # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'entra_auth'

and this can:

from .entra_auth import EntraAuth

The loader puts / on sys.path, not /app, so the flat import has nowhere to
resolve from. The relative import works in both contexts — inside the container
and when the repo's unit tests import the same module as
google_adk_client.entra_auth.

The other half of the same mistake: a COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock agent.py ./
line that never mentions entra_auth.py, so the module is not in the image at
all. Nothing fails at build time — the import is what fails.

Both are invisible to a green test suite, because the tests import
google_adk_client.entra_auth from the source tree, and the source tree is not
what ships. Loading the reconstructed /app layout is a two-line check that
catches both:

from google.adk.cli.utils.agent_loader import AgentLoader
AgentLoader("/app").load_agent("app")   # ModuleNotFoundError before the fix
Deploying It

Order matters, because the ADK client needs an endpoint that does not exist
until the master is up and A2A is enabled on it:

./infra/deploy_foundry_master.sh          # provision, deploy, then PATCH incoming A2A on
export FOUNDRY_MASTER_A2A_ENDPOINT="https://.../endpoint/protocols/a2a"
export GCP_PROJECT="your-project" AZURE_TENANT_ID="..." AZURE_CLIENT_ID="..."
./infra/deploy_google_adk_client.sh       # ADK proxy on Cloud Run, secret from Secret Manager

The enable script prints the resolved card and the endpoint to export, so the
second step is a copy-paste rather than a URL you assemble by hand.

Two Things That Only Broke When It Ran

The unit tests were green the whole time. Neither of these was visible to them.

The v1.0 method name is not the v0.3 method name. A hand-written JSON-RPC
call using message/send — the v0.3 spelling that most A2A examples still show
— comes back as:

{"error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found",
           "data": [{"reason": "METHOD_NOT_FOUND",
                     "metadata": {"detail": "'method' field is not a valid A2A method."}}]}}

In a2a-sdk 1.x the JSON-RPC method is SendMessage, with proto-JSON params.
Worth knowing that the Foundry card advertises three interfaces on the same
URL — JSONRPC 1.0, JSONRPC 0.3, and HTTP+JSON 0.3 — so the server is not the
thing constraining you; your client's spelling is.

The container needed a dependency nothing declared. azure.identity.aio
builds its async transport with aiohttp, which is not a hard dependency of
azure-identity. It is present on a normal workstation, so local runs pass. In
a uv sync --frozen container it is absent, the build succeeds, and the first
token request dies:

File "azure/core/pipeline/transport/__init__.py", line 94, in __getattr__
    raise ImportError("aiohttp package is not installed")

Both bugs share a shape: the lockfile and the source tree that tests run against
are not the artifact that ships.

Results

All figures below are from the live deployment — Cloud Run in us-central1
calling a Foundry master in eastus2, gpt-5-mini, live Frankfurter rates, the
prompt Convert 250 GBP to USD and JPY.

Measurement Value Authenticated agent-card GET (warm median, 6 runs) 0.35 s Same, first fetch 0.51 s A2A SendMessage, workstation → master (warm median, 6 runs) 21.2 s A2A round trip via the Cloud Run ADK client (median, 5 runs) 23.4 s Same, range 18.9 s – 29.5 s First request against a fresh Cloud Run revision 20.8 s

Every run returned the same numbers, and they are the right ones:

{"source_currency":"GBP","target_currency":"USD","rate":"1.3389",
 "converted_amount":"334.7250","source":"frankfurter-live"}
{"source_currency":"GBP","target_currency":"JPY","rate":"218.15",
 "converted_amount":"54537.50","source":"frankfurter-live"}

Three things stand out.

Authenticated discovery is cheap. The worry going in was that a card fetch
requiring a token and a role check would be meaningfully more expensive than an
anonymous GET. At 0.35 s warm it is noise next to the call it precedes, and
the token is cached across calls anyway.

The ADK proxy hop costs about 2 seconds — 21.2 s direct versus 23.4 s
through Cloud Run, against a spread of 18.9–29.5 s. Put plainly, the run-to-run
variance of the master is larger than the entire cost of putting a second cloud
in the path.

The master dominates everything. Roughly 20 seconds of a 23-second round
trip is gpt-5-mini deciding to call convert_currency twice and waiting on
Frankfurter each time. If you want this architecture faster, the protocol and
the proxy are not where the time is. Note the contrast with the previous
article's Azure-orchestrating-Google numbers (a2a_only at 1.69 s median):
same protocol, same clouds, an order of magnitude apart — because there the
remote agent answered one question, and here the master runs a multi-tool
reasoning loop. Protocol overhead is not what you are measuring in either case.

Infrastructure timings, for anyone budgeting a first deploy: azd provision
64 s, azd deploy 116 s, and — the one that will confuse you — 105 seconds
before data-plane RBAC took effect. Agent writes kept returning 403 with the
role assignment already visible in az role assignment list. It is propagation,
not misconfiguration. Wait it out before you start re-assigning roles.

Raw results are in evaluations/results/foundry-master-live-2026-07-31.json,
and evaluations/measure_foundry_master.py regenerates them.

One caveat on scope: these are single-prompt samples, not a distribution. The
38-case evaluation matrix from the previous article has not been re-run against
this architecture yet.

Lessons
  1. Making Foundry the master is an auth problem, not a protocol problem. The JSON-RPC half is the easy half whichever cloud is in charge. Budget your time for identity — and for RBAC propagation, which took 105 seconds here while the assignment already showed as present.
  2. Discovery is not always free — but it is cheap. An authenticated agent card makes every "card not found" a role assignment until proven otherwise. It costs 0.35 s warm, which is not the thing to optimize.
  3. protocol_configuration replaces, it does not merge. Verified, not assumed: patching a2a alone dropped Responses and took the A2A card down with it (400), and the request that did it returned 200. Send every protocol you want to keep, and pin it with a test.
  4. Hosted runtimes flatten your repo layout. An MCP stdio tool spawns a real subprocess with a real import path — if your deploy bundle is a subdirectory, the imports have to be inside it.
  5. Cross-cloud credentials live on the calling side. Google calling Azure means an Azure client secret in Google Secret Manager. There is no way around the secret; there is a way around having it in your source tree.
  6. Get the token audience right before you debug anything else. A valid token for the wrong scope fails in a way that looks like a permissions bug.
  7. Injectable HTTP clients are what make cross-vendor agents cheap. ADK's RemoteA2aAgent taking an httpx_client is the difference between an adapter and a fork.
  8. Your tests import the source tree; your users run the image. A missing COPY line, a flat import that only works outside a package, and a transitive dependency your workstation happens to have (aiohttp) were all invisible to a green test suite. Load the container's real layout, or deploy and call it — those are the only two things that find this class of bug.
  9. Check the method name before you check your permissions. message/send is v0.3; SendMessage is v1.x. The failure is METHOD_NOT_FOUND on an endpoint you are fully authorized to call.
  10. The protocol is never the slow part. ~20 s of a 23 s round trip was the master's own reasoning and tool calls. The second cloud cost about 2 s — less than the master's run-to-run variance.
Source

Both role assignments, the deploy scripts, and the tests:

GitHub - xbill9/foundry-adk-a2a-currency

The Foundry-as-master components are foundry_master/, google_adk_client/,
and infra/enable_foundry_master_a2a.py. Measurements come from
evaluations/measure_foundry_master.py, raw output in
evaluations/results/foundry-master-live-2026-07-31.json. The setup where
Google hosts the remote agent, along with its benchmark results, is in the
previous article in this series.

If you have run incoming A2A on a hosted Foundry agent — especially if your
numbers differ, or you found a preview quirk this missed — I would like to
compare notes.

items.title: Foundry as Master, Bedrock as Remote: The Smoke Test Finally Passed
items.summary:
I wanted one specific piece of coverage: Microsoft Foundry (master)
    ├── MCP ──> live exchange-rate baseline
    └── A2A ──> Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (remote specialist) On July 30, 2026, that direction worked end to end. This matters because I had already tested the reverse topology—AgentCore as coordinator and Foundry as remote. A cross-cloud claim based on only one direction is weak. This run proves Foundry can own the request, execute its local MCP baseline, call an AgentCore A2A agent, and apply deterministic verification. The code and sanitized evidence are in xbill9/foundry-bedrock-a2a-currency . What actually passed The input was 100 USD → EUR . I invoked the Foundry-hosted coordinator through its Responses endpoint in all three benchmark modes: Mode Path Observed result Adapter time mcp_only Foundry → local MCP 87.13800 EUR 359 ms a2a_only Foundry → A2A → AgentCore 87.138 EUR 25,105 ms verified both paths concurrently exact agreement 28,163 ms The verified result reported: { "relative_difference" : "0" , "agreed" : true , "failures" : {} } That is one smoke case, not a latency distribution and not a completed benchmark matrix. The useful conclusion is narrower: the Foundry-master cloud boundary works, including authentication, discovery, invocation, and deterministic comparison. The repository also passes 66 deterministic tests; one optional integration test is skipped without its external dependency. The model does not do the math Currency conversion makes interoperability easy to falsify. Every quote carries the amount, rate, converted amount, observation time, source, and adapter latency. Money and rates use Python Decimal . The coordinator—not an LLM—checks agreement: difference = abs ( primary . converted_amount - verifier . converted_amount ) relative_difference = difference / abs ( primary . converted_amount ) agreed = relative_difference <= Decimal ( " 0.005 " ) The model handles intent and chooses one tool call. Framework-independent code owns arithmetic, concurrency, timeout policy, and failure reporting. The boundary that survived the flip The stable application depends on two interfaces: an MCP-backed ExchangeRateTool ; an A2A-backed RemoteCurrencyAgent . Microsoft Agent Framework and Foundry hosting sit outside those interfaces. Strands and AgentCore sit outside them on the other side. Flipping the clouds did not require rewriting the domain service. That is more valuable than merely getting two SDKs into one process. Each cloud can be deployed independently, and the benchmark can still compare MCP-only, A2A-only, and verified execution. Authentication was the real cross-cloud problem AgentCore's default runtime authorization is IAM/SigV4. That is appropriate for AWS callers, but a Foundry-hosted container does not automatically have AWS credentials. For this test I configured AgentCore with a custom JWT authorizer and used a Cognito machine-to-machine client: Foundry container
    ├── client_credentials ──> Cognito token endpoint
    └── Bearer JWT ──────────> AgentCore A2A runtime The coordinator's A2A adapter now supports OAuth client credentials, caches the token until shortly before expiry, and retains static bearer support for other peer profiles. The AgentCore authorizer validates the issuer, client, and required currencybench/invoke scope. No token participates in the domain layer. What broke before the green run The successful diagram hides most of the work. These were observed failures, not hypothetical risks. 1. AgentCore's A2A server and the client wanted different SDK generations The coordinator client uses A2A 1.x. AgentCore's A2A extra currently requires the 0.3 line in the deployed server bundle. Installing both into the same bundle produced an unsatisfiable dependency graph. The fix was architectural: pin the AgentCore application bundle to its compatible A2A SDK while keeping the Foundry-side client separate. The network protocol interoperated even though the Python packages did not share a version. 2. IAM authorization did not cross the cloud boundary A direct AWS CLI invocation worked, but the Foundry container could not sign an AWS request. Switching the runtime to custom JWT authorization and adding the OAuth adapter made the remote callable without embedding AWS credentials. 3. The default ten-second timeout was false confidence The first hosted a2a_only call failed cleanly: { "failures" : { "a2a" : "timeout: adapter timed out" }, "elapsed_ms" : 10010 } A direct remote call had already taken about 25 seconds. The adapter was working; the benchmark policy was too aggressive for a cold cross-cloud path. The hosted timeout is now 60 seconds. The next A2A-only invocation completed in 25.1 seconds. 4. Foundry's source build could not find its image The hosted-agent remote build repeatedly ended with ImageError: Container image not found . I switched to a prebuilt, digest-pinned image in Azure Container Registry. The next failure was more precise: registry authentication. Three identities were visible—the Foundry account, the project, and the per-agent runtime identity. Image pull uses the project managed identity . Granting the other two AcrPull did not help. The deployment became active after: enabling ACR authentication-as-ARM; granting the project identity repository-reader/pull access; and redeploying the same digest-pinned image. 5. Azure resource state and RBAC both had memory A soft-deleted Foundry account blocked recreation until it was purged. Project role assignments also took time to propagate. Those are deployment-plane facts, distinct from whether A2A works at runtime. The smoke result In verified mode, Foundry started both adapters. Its MCP leg returned rate 0.87138 ; the AgentCore specialist returned rate 0.87138 . Deterministic code computed a relative difference of zero and marked the quotes as agreed. The MCP result also carried a stale-observation warning. The coordinator preserved it rather than letting the model smooth it away. The hosted response took about 45 seconds end to end while the measured adapter work took 28.2 seconds. That gap includes model and hosted-response overhead. With one observation, it would be irresponsible to call either number a benchmark. What this proves—and what it does not Observed: Foundry hosted the master coordinator. Foundry's MCP-only path completed. Foundry acquired an OAuth token and invoked AgentCore over A2A. AgentCore returned a structured currency quote. Verified mode ran both paths and reported exact agreement. The three-mode smoke completed without adapter failures after the timeout
correction. Not yet established: warm and cold latency distributions; behavior under throttling or token expiry; a full multi-currency matrix; production secret rotation and availability controls; superiority of either framework or cloud. That distinction is the point of the project. The result is coverage, not a victory lap: Microsoft Foundry works as the main cloud, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore works as its authenticated remote A2A specialist.
items.summary_html:
I wanted one specific piece of coverage:

Microsoft Foundry (master)
    ├── MCP ──> live exchange-rate baseline
    └── A2A ──> Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (remote specialist)

On July 30, 2026, that direction worked end to end.

This matters because I had already tested the reverse topology—AgentCore as
coordinator and Foundry as remote. A cross-cloud claim based on only one
direction is weak. This run proves Foundry can own the request, execute its
local MCP baseline, call an AgentCore A2A agent, and apply deterministic
verification.

The code and sanitized evidence are in
xbill9/foundry-bedrock-a2a-currency.

What actually passed

The input was 100 USD → EUR. I invoked the Foundry-hosted coordinator through
its Responses endpoint in all three benchmark modes:

Mode Path Observed result Adapter time mcp_only Foundry → local MCP 87.13800 EUR 359 ms a2a_only Foundry → A2A → AgentCore 87.138 EUR 25,105 ms verified both paths concurrently exact agreement 28,163 ms

The verified result reported:

{
  "relative_difference": "0",
  "agreed": true,
  "failures": {}
}

That is one smoke case, not a latency distribution and not a completed
benchmark matrix. The useful conclusion is narrower: the Foundry-master cloud
boundary works, including authentication, discovery, invocation, and
deterministic comparison.

The repository also passes 66 deterministic tests; one optional integration
test is skipped without its external dependency.

The model does not do the math

Currency conversion makes interoperability easy to falsify. Every quote carries
the amount, rate, converted amount, observation time, source, and adapter
latency. Money and rates use Python Decimal.

The coordinator—not an LLM—checks agreement:

difference = abs(primary.converted_amount - verifier.converted_amount)
relative_difference = difference / abs(primary.converted_amount)
agreed = relative_difference <= Decimal("0.005")

The model handles intent and chooses one tool call. Framework-independent code
owns arithmetic, concurrency, timeout policy, and failure reporting.

The boundary that survived the flip

The stable application depends on two interfaces:

  • an MCP-backed ExchangeRateTool;
  • an A2A-backed RemoteCurrencyAgent.

Microsoft Agent Framework and Foundry hosting sit outside those interfaces.
Strands and AgentCore sit outside them on the other side. Flipping the clouds
did not require rewriting the domain service.

That is more valuable than merely getting two SDKs into one process. Each cloud
can be deployed independently, and the benchmark can still compare MCP-only,
A2A-only, and verified execution.

Authentication was the real cross-cloud problem

AgentCore's default runtime authorization is IAM/SigV4. That is appropriate for
AWS callers, but a Foundry-hosted container does not automatically have AWS
credentials.

For this test I configured AgentCore with a custom JWT authorizer and used a
Cognito machine-to-machine client:

Foundry container
    ├── client_credentials ──> Cognito token endpoint
    └── Bearer JWT ──────────> AgentCore A2A runtime

The coordinator's A2A adapter now supports OAuth client credentials, caches the
token until shortly before expiry, and retains static bearer support for other
peer profiles. The AgentCore authorizer validates the issuer, client, and
required currencybench/invoke scope.

No token participates in the domain layer.

What broke before the green run

The successful diagram hides most of the work. These were observed failures,
not hypothetical risks.

1. AgentCore's A2A server and the client wanted different SDK generations

The coordinator client uses A2A 1.x. AgentCore's A2A extra currently requires
the 0.3 line in the deployed server bundle. Installing both into the same
bundle produced an unsatisfiable dependency graph.

The fix was architectural: pin the AgentCore application bundle to its
compatible A2A SDK while keeping the Foundry-side client separate. The network
protocol interoperated even though the Python packages did not share a
version.

2. IAM authorization did not cross the cloud boundary

A direct AWS CLI invocation worked, but the Foundry container could not sign an
AWS request. Switching the runtime to custom JWT authorization and adding the
OAuth adapter made the remote callable without embedding AWS credentials.

3. The default ten-second timeout was false confidence

The first hosted a2a_only call failed cleanly:

{
  "failures": {
    "a2a": "timeout: adapter timed out"
  },
  "elapsed_ms": 10010
}

A direct remote call had already taken about 25 seconds. The adapter was
working; the benchmark policy was too aggressive for a cold cross-cloud path.
The hosted timeout is now 60 seconds. The next A2A-only invocation completed in
25.1 seconds.

4. Foundry's source build could not find its image

The hosted-agent remote build repeatedly ended with ImageError: Container
image not found. I switched to a prebuilt, digest-pinned image in Azure
Container Registry.

The next failure was more precise: registry authentication. Three identities
were visible—the Foundry account, the project, and the per-agent runtime
identity. Image pull uses the project managed identity. Granting the other
two AcrPull did not help.

The deployment became active after:

  • enabling ACR authentication-as-ARM;
  • granting the project identity repository-reader/pull access; and
  • redeploying the same digest-pinned image.
5. Azure resource state and RBAC both had memory

A soft-deleted Foundry account blocked recreation until it was purged. Project
role assignments also took time to propagate. Those are deployment-plane
facts, distinct from whether A2A works at runtime.

The smoke result

In verified mode, Foundry started both adapters. Its MCP leg returned rate
0.87138; the AgentCore specialist returned rate 0.87138. Deterministic code
computed a relative difference of zero and marked the quotes as agreed.

The MCP result also carried a stale-observation warning. The coordinator
preserved it rather than letting the model smooth it away.

The hosted response took about 45 seconds end to end while the measured adapter
work took 28.2 seconds. That gap includes model and hosted-response overhead.
With one observation, it would be irresponsible to call either number a
benchmark.

What this proves—and what it does not

Observed:

  • Foundry hosted the master coordinator.
  • Foundry's MCP-only path completed.
  • Foundry acquired an OAuth token and invoked AgentCore over A2A.
  • AgentCore returned a structured currency quote.
  • Verified mode ran both paths and reported exact agreement.
  • The three-mode smoke completed without adapter failures after the timeout correction.

Not yet established:

  • warm and cold latency distributions;
  • behavior under throttling or token expiry;
  • a full multi-currency matrix;
  • production secret rotation and availability controls;
  • superiority of either framework or cloud.

That distinction is the point of the project. The result is coverage, not a
victory lap: Microsoft Foundry works as the main cloud, and Amazon Bedrock
AgentCore works as its authenticated remote A2A specialist.
