items.title: Rivers, railroads, and political bribes: How every state capital was chosen
items.summary: Jackson is Mississippi's capital because of its central location in the state. Sean Pavone/Getty Images/iStockphoto Most states have had multiple capital cities throughout their histories. Most commonly, geography and transportation links were the biggest factors in determining a capital. Most capitals have been decided through legislative or statewide votes. From railroad hubs and river towns to hard-fought votes and alleged bribes, America's state capitals took wildly different paths to power. Today, in 17 states, the capital is also the most populous city. Phoenix , the nation's most populous state capital, has more than 1.6 million residents, while Montpelier, Vermont, has fewer than 8,000, according to the latest Census estimates. But population was often far from the deciding factor when designating a state capital. Many were selected hundreds of years ago, when some of today's cities were little more than stretches of undeveloped land. Some were simply designated as state capitals by legislative or popular vote, while others were subject to political trickery and corruption, and some were chosen because they were the sites of new, booming industries. In a few cases, townspeople even chipped in to fund the new capitol buildings . Most commonly, cities were chosen based on their geographic location. Before modern transportation, rivers and railroads were the best means of transit. As such, many state capitals sit along rivers or were chosen for their central locations to allow legislators to travel easily from every corner of the state. From Alabama to Wyoming, see how every state's capital earned the title. ALABAMA: Montgomery Montgomery, Alabama. fotoguy22/Getty Images Though Alabama became a state in 1819, Montgomery didn't become its capital until 1846. Before statehood, the territorial capital was located in the town of St. Stephens, chosen for its proximity to the Tombigbee River, according to the Montgomery Advertiser . The capital soon changed to Huntsville, then Cahaba and Tuscaloosa, after statehood. Montgomery was finally decided upon for its central location amid changes in the state's transportation, economy, and geography, the Advertiser reported. ALASKA: Juneau Juneau, Alaska. JillianCain/Getty Images Anchorage is Alaska's most populous city with nearly 300,000 residents, per the most recent Census estimates. But Alaska's capital sits more than 500 miles southeast in the small city of Juneau. Juneau's initial growth came in part from its booming gold-mining industry. When it became the new capital of territorial Alaska in 1906, it was Alaska's biggest city, according to KTOO . The capital city was previously Sitka, which sits on an island in Alaska's Alexander Archipelago. In Juneau's 120-year history as Alaska's capital, many efforts in the state legislature have been made to move the capital to Anchorage, largely because of travel difficulties for elected officials. In 1974, voters approved an initiative to relocate the capital, but subsequent proposals to finance the move were rejected, KTOO reported. ARIZONA: Phoenix Phoenix, Arizona. Leonid Andronov/Getty Images Arizona's territorial capital moved from Prescott to Tucson, back to Prescott, and finally to Phoenix in 1889, per KJZZ Phoenix . Phoenix, originally founded as Swilling's Mill in 1867 by a Confederate veteran, started to expand toward the end of the 19th century. It was chosen as the capital in 1889 due to its growing significance in transportation and agriculture. It wasn't until 1912 that Arizona became a state. Today, Phoenix is home to 1.67 million residents and is the most populous state capital in the US. ARKANSAS: Little Rock Little Rock, Arkansas. ChrisBoswell/Getty Images/iStockphoto When Arkansas was a territory, its capital sat in Arkansas Post, a location which held significance during French and Spanish control of the area, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas . However, it was also the site of flooding and illnesses like malaria. Little Rock was chosen as the territory's capital in 1821 largely due to interest from settlers. Located along the Arkansas River, the new settlement allowed for travel via the Mississippi River. Arkansas was granted statehood 15 years later. CALIFORNIA: Sacramento Sacramento, California. casch/Getty Images/iStockphoto Though Monterey served as California's capital during Spanish and Mexican rule, San Jose was the first designated capital when California became a US state, per the California Capitol Museum . The capital moved to Vallejo before Sacramento was chosen for its proximity to rivers, as well as the infrastructure and transportation links it already had in place. Just two months after moving its headquarters to Sacramento, the state government was forced to move back to Vallejo due to flooding. The capital later moved to Benicia before permanently returning to Sacramento. COLORADO: Denver Denver, Colorado. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images Before Colorado was a state, Colorado City and Golden served as its capital cities in the 1860s. Denver, becoming a growing population center and commercial hub, was picked as the temporary capital in 1876. In 1881, voters chose to keep Denver as the capital in a referendum, according to the Colorado State Capitol Visitor Guide . CONNECTICUT: Hartford Hartford, Connecticut. ChrisBoswell/Getty Images Connecticut's capital history dates back to the turn of the 18th century. In 1701, the Connecticut Colony's General Court established two capital cities: Hartford and New Haven. General Assembly meetings would alternate between the two locations, according to Connecticut History . In the 1870s, the state held a referendum to choose between the two cities, citing the impracticality of the current system. Hartford won out and officially became the state's capital in 1875. DELAWARE: Dover Dover, Delaware. hyderabadi/Getty Images/iStockphoto Delaware's capital came about as a direct result of the Revolutionary War . As the British moved to seize territory in Delaware in 1777, the capital of New Castle was moved to Dover over safety concerns and for its strategic central location, per Delaware Historical & Cultural Affairs . FLORIDA: Tallahassee Tallahassee, Florida. Aneese/Getty Images/iStockphoto Like Connecticut, Florida originally had two capitals. When it first became a US territory, lawmakers would alternate between St. Augustine and Pensacola, which are nearly 400 miles apart. Travel was dangerous and would take weeks, according to the Florida Department of State . Legislators decided to meet in the middle for Florida's new capital. They chose Tallahassee, the midway point between the two cities, in 1824. GEORGIA: Atlanta Atlanta, Georgia. felixmizioznikov/Getty Images Before Atlanta was chosen as Georgia's capital in the 1870s, a handful of other cities had held the designation. Savannah, Augusta, Louisville, and Milledgeville were all Georgia's capital at one point, with the latter holding the title for 60 years, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia . Atlanta was ultimately chosen because of its significance as a railroad hub. HAWAII: Honolulu Honolulu, Hawaii. mj0007/Getty Images/iStockphoto Honolulu's status as Hawaii's capital dates to half a century before the islands were annexed by the US. In 1845, Hawaii's monarch, King Kamehameha III, moved the royal buildings from Lahaina, on the island of Maui, to Honolulu due to its harbor and growing commerce, and its easier access for visiting dignitaries. After the government was overthrown in 1893, the provisional government and then the Republic of Hawaii continued to operate out of the city, per the National Park Service . It remained the capital after Hawaii became a state in 1959. IDAHO: Boise Boise, Idaho. Seibel Photography LLC/Getty Images/iStockphoto When Idaho was established as a US territory in 1863, Lewiston initially served as its capital. This was soon changed to Boise because of a population and mining boom in the city. When the change was made, soldiers forcefully entered the capitol building in Lewiston and transported the territorial seal and papers to Boise. Today, some residents of Lewiston still believe their city's status as the capital was "stolen," the Idaho Press reported. ILLINOIS: Springfield Springfield, Illinois. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Illinois' original capital was Kaskaskia, located along the Mississippi River. Vandalia then served as the capital for two decades before an effort in the state legislature led by a young Abraham Lincoln resulted in Springfield being named the capital, according to the Illinois Secretary of State . The gradual move northward reflected a growing population in the northern half of the state. INDIANA: Indianapolis Indianapolis, Indiana. RudyBalasko/Getty Images/iStockphoto Corydon was Indiana's original capital when it was a territory and during its early years of statehood. In the 1820s, Indianapolis was established as the state's new capital for its central location, per the Indiana Historical Society . IOWA: Des Moines Des Moines, Iowa. Jacob Boomsma/Getty Images/iStockphoto When Iowa became a territory in 1838, Burlington served as its capital, and it was soon replaced by Iowa City. However, legislators quickly desired a more central location for the capital, according to Iowa PBS . Fort Des Moines, as it was known at the time, was chosen because it sat within 2 miles of the intersection of the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers. KANSAS: Topeka Topeka, Kansas. MattGush/Getty Images During the state's territorial struggle over slavery, Lecompton, Leavenworth, Pawnee, and present-day Fairway all spent time as the capital of Kansas for different governments, in addition to Lawrence serving as the then-territory's de facto capital from 1858 to 1861, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported. Topeka was first chosen as the temporary capital in 1859, and it was made permanent in an election-day vote two years later, per the Kansas Historical Society . KENTUCKY: Frankfort Frankfort, Kentucky. Sean Pavone/Getty Images/iStockphoto Since Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort has served as the Bluegrass State's capital. While different cities vied for capital status, Frankfort won in part because its supporters offered gold and even a log cabin to the commissioners overseeing the decision, per the Kentucky Historical Society . LOUISIANA: Baton Rouge Baton Rouge, Lousiana. CRobertson/Getty Images Baton Rouge sits as Louisiana's capital because of a deliberate effort to shift power away from New Orleans, according to the museum Louisiana's Old State Capitol . Per the museum, in 1845, "a new state constitution mandated the location be 'not less than 60 miles from the city of New Orleans.'" Baton Rouge sits along the Mississippi River, roughly 80 miles northeast of New Orleans. From 1829 to 1831, Donaldsonville briefly served as the state's capital, according to the city . MAINE: Augusta Augusta, Maine. HABesen/Getty Images Maine's capital was originally Portland, currently the state's largest city. However, the city's coastal location was the cause of concern in the 1820s, with some worrying it was vulnerable to attack, News Center Maine reported. Maine's legislature sought a more central location in the state, eventually choosing Augusta, partly because the city offered to pay for construction of a capitol building. MARYLAND: Annapolis Annapolis, Maryland. Amy Sparwasser/Getty Images In colonial times, Maryland's capital was the town of St. Mary's City, located near the base of the Potomac River. Near the end of the 17th century, the colony's general assembly moved the capital to Anne Arundel Town — now known as Annapolis — due to population growth in the northern part of the colony, according to Maryland State Archives . MASSACHUSETTS: Boston Boston, Massachusetts. ChrisBoswell/Getty Images/iStockphoto Boston is one of the oldest capitals in the US, holding the title in Massachusetts for nearly 400 years. The city was designated as the capital of the Massachusetts Bay Colony when Puritan settlers, led by John Winthrop, established it in the 1630s. Winthrop first settled in Salem before moving to Boston, according to the Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth . MICHIGAN: Lansing Lansing, Michigan. fotoguy22/Getty Images Having originally served as Michigan's territorial capital, Detroit was chosen as Michigan's capital after statehood was granted in the 1830s. This was a temporary measure, however, with Michigan's constitution noting it would serve as the capital "until the year eighteen-hundred and forty-seven, when it shall be permanently located by the Legislature," according to the Michigan State Capitol . The empty space that would later become Lansing was chosen, even though people at the time called it a "howling wilderness," according to the Capitol. Legislators met in a temporary wooden building before the town was constructed, and it wasn't until 1859 that it was incorporated as a city. Lansing was chosen for its central location, according to Downtown Lansing Inc . MINNESOTA: St. Paul Saint Paul, Minnesota. AndreyKrav/Getty Images/iStockphoto St. Paul has served as Minnesota's capital since it became a US territory in 1849, according to the Minnesota Historical Society . It was likely chosen for its location along the Mississippi River and the area's population growth. In 1857, a bill in Minnesota's territorial legislature threatened to move the capital to St. Peter. Legislator Joseph Rolette, once he was in possession of the bill, intentionally went missing to prevent its passage. While Rolette is often credited with preventing the move from taking place, the incident was largely symbolic as the bill also failed to pass on legal grounds, per the Minnesota Historical Society. MISSISSIPPI: Jackson Jackson, Mississippi. SeanPavonePhoto/Getty Images/iStockphoto The towns of Natchez, Washington, and Columbia all at one point served as the capital of Mississippi when it was a territory and in its early statehood, the Clarion-Ledger reported . Like other states, however, legislators sought a more central location for the capital. The location that became Jackson was chosen because it sat at the intersection of trade routes, per Mississippi History Now . Incorporated in 1822, the city was named after Andrew Jackson. MISSOURI: Jefferson City Jefferson City, Missouri. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images St. Louis originally served as the capital of the Missouri territory before St. Charles was named the temporary capital when Missouri became a state in 1821. Jefferson City, then an undeveloped site, was picked as "a compromise between two major population centers," according to the city . It has served as Missouri's capital since 1826. MONTANA: Helena Helena, Montana. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images The capital of Montana was set to be decided by voters in the election of 1892. Seven cities competed, and while the election didn't produce a winner, it left Anaconda and Helena as the clear frontrunners, according to Visit Southwest Montana . People in both cities campaigned for the capital, with a winner to be decided in the election of 1894. Helena was victorious, winning by a margin of just 1.8% — fewer than 2,000 votes. NEBRASKA: Lincoln Lincoln, Nebraska. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images While Omaha had served as Nebraska's capital when it was a territory, many Nebraskans wanted a change, according to the Nebraska State Historical Society . A new site — named Lincoln after the recently assassinated president — was chosen southwest of Omaha, in part because it was south of Nebraska's Platte River, which was difficult to cross at the time, and most of the population lived south of the river. NEVADA: Carson City Carson City, Nevada, pabradyphoto/Getty Images Carson City has always served as Nevada's capital. The city was settled as a proper community in 1858. In 1859, the area saw a commercial boom after gold and silver were discovered nearby, per Visit Carson City. In 1861, it was named the territorial capital, and it remained the capital when Nevada became a state in 1864. NEW HAMPSHIRE: Concord Concord, New Hampshire. Sanghwan Kim/Getty Images Before Concord, other cities, such as Exeter, served as New Hampshire's capital, according to the Exeter Historical Society . Concord became the capital in 1808 for its central location, according to the city . NEW JERSEY: Trenton Trenton, New Jersey. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images Like many other state capitals, Trenton was chosen as New Jersey's capital city in 1790 largely due to geographic factors. The city is located between New York City and Philadelphia and sits along the Delaware River, which was significant for trade and transportation, per Trenton Daily . NEW MEXICO: Santa Fe Santa Fe, New Mexico. 4nadia/Getty Images Spanish colonists established Santa Fe as the capital of Nuevo México in 1610. It then continued to serve as the capital of the province under Mexican rule, and later the capital of the US territory and state, according to Tourism Santa Fe . NEW YORK: Albany Albany, New York. BRULIN REMI/Getty Images While Kingston briefly served as New York's first capital, the city was burned down by the British during the Revolutionary War. Albany, farther up the Hudson River, held significance during the war for its role in military planning and the distribution of supplies. For these reasons, Albany was named New York's capital in 1797, News 10 New York reported . NORTH CAROLINA: Raleigh Raleigh, North Carolina. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images The cities of Bath, Edenton, and New Bern all served as the capital of North Carolina before Raleigh was chosen. The latter, then just a grove of trees, was ultimately selected as the permanent capital in 1792 because of its central location, North Carolina's Our State Magazine reported. NORTH DAKOTA: Bismarck Bismarck, North Dakota. 4nadia/Getty Images/iStockphoto When North and South Dakota were unified as the Dakota Territory, Yankton — now in South Dakota — originally served as its capital. However, many Dakotans thought it was too far away from the growing cities of Deadwood and Fargo. Additionally, Yankton didn't sit along a transcontinental railroad line, according to North Dakota Studies . In the 1880s, a commission was appointed to locate a new suitable capital for the territory. The process was plagued by corruption, including members of the commission being given financial incentives to vote for Bismarck. The northern city won and remained the capital of North Dakota when the Dakotas were admitted to the Union as separate states. OHIO: Columbus Columbus, Ohio. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images/iStockphoto Chillicothe served as Ohio's original capital when statehood was granted, and Zanesville later acted as the state's temporary capital. However, a piece of legislation in 1810 ordered that a permanent capital must be "not more than 40 miles from what may be deemed the common center of the state," according to the Ohio Statehouse . This meant a new capital was to be chosen. The site that would become Columbus was picked in 1812 for its central location. OKLAHOMA: Oklahoma City Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. benkrut/Getty Images/iStockphoto Guthrie originally served as Oklahoma's territorial capital and later its state capital. However, Oklahoma City was seeing rapid growth and became the state's leading population center, prompting a statewide vote to make the city Oklahoma's capital. The vote was successful, and Oklahoma City became the capital in 1910, according to the Oklahoma Historical Society . OREGON: Salem Salem, Oregon. 4nadia/Getty Images/iStockphoto When Oregon was a territory, Oregon City initially served as its capital. Salem took over as capital in 1851, and, as a compromise, other cities, such as Portland, were given other public institutions, according to the Willamette Heritage Center . Even after Salem remained the capital when Oregon achieved statehood, many citizens and legislators were unhappy with the choice. Following a wave of legal challenges and efforts to move the capital elsewhere, elections in 1862 and 1864 finalized the city as the state's capital. PENNSYLVANIA: Harrisburg Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Mak Studio/Getty Images William Penn originally chose Philadelphia as the capital of Pennsylvania in the 17th century, a status it held until 1799. During the Revolutionary War, the Second Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence in the state house, now known as Independence Hall, according to the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission . The capital was moved west to Lancaster, and later to Harrisburg in 1812, for lawmakers to convene in a more central location. RHODE ISLAND: Providence Providence, Rhode Island. Ray Tan/Getty Images Like other states, Rhode Island had multiple capitals. Legislators alternated between county state houses in five different towns — Providence, Newport, Bristol, East Greenwich, and Kingston — for sessions until 1854, when it was narrowed down to Newport and Providence, according to Newport History . As Providence's influence grew, it was named the state's sole capital in 1900. SOUTH CAROLINA: Columbia Columbia, South Carolina. Kruck20/Getty Images Charleston originally served as South Carolina's capital, but a 1786 assembly vote changed it to Columbia. The city's central location made it a more desirable capital than coastal Charleston, according to the South Carolina Statehouse . SOUTH DAKOTA: Pierre Pierre, South Dakota. Gabriel Shakour/Getty Images/iStockphoto Even though Yankton, the original capital of the Dakota Territory, was located in the new state of South Dakota, it was never considered for the capital when the state was admitted into the Union in 1889. Pierre, which is in the middle of the state and located on the Missouri River, was chosen as a temporary capital that year, Dakota News Now reported . It remained as the capital after it received the most votes in an 1890 statewide election. TENNESSEE: Nashville Nashville, Tennessee. Nicholas Klein/Getty Images After Tennessee became a state, Knoxville, Kingston, Nashville, and Murfreesboro all served as its capital at one point. It wasn't until an 1843 Tennessee General Assembly vote that Nashville was named the permanent capital. The decision was likely due to the city's commercial and cultural status, as well as its central location in the state, according to Nashville Adventures . TEXAS: Austin Austin, Texas. CrackerClips/Getty Images/iStockphoto The area that became Texas had different capitals at different times under Spanish and Mexican rule. When Texas was an independent republic from 1836 to 1846, it also had several capitals, most notably Houston and Austin. The latter — originally called Waterloo — remained the capital when Texas was annexed by the US, per the Texas Almanac . UTAH: Salt Lake City Salt Lake City, Utah. miroslav_1/Getty Images/iStockphoto When Utah was a territory, a small town in the middle of the state called Fillmore — named after the 13th US president — was designated as the capital. However, the town's expected growth never materialized, and the more populous and commercially successful Salt Lake City was designated as the territory's new capital in the 1850s, per the Utah History Encyclopedia . VERMONT: Montpelier Montpelier, Vermont. 4nadia/Getty Images/iStockphoto Vermont didn't have a proper capital until the 19th century, when Montpelier was chosen in 1805, the Vermont Daily Chronicle reported . Before then, legislators would alternate between 14 different locations. Montpelier was decided upon because of its central location, as well as the town's citizens personally raising funds to build the capitol. VIRGINIA: Richmond Richmond, Virginia. eurobanks/Getty Images/iStockphoto Jamestown served as the original capital of the Colony of Virginia for most of the 17th century, before the capital was moved to Williamsburg in 1699, according to the Virginia General Assembly . During the Revolutionary War, Thomas Jefferson, then the governor of Virginia, led an effort to move the capital to Richmond, and it officially became the capital in 1780. Supporters cited it as safer than Williamsburg from a potential British attack while still sitting along a river (although British forces would attack the city in 1781) and more centrally located for the state's growing population. WASHINGTON: Olympia Olympia, Washington. ChrisBoswell/Getty Images/iStockphoto Olympia's status as Washington's capital dates back to when the Evergreen State was still a territory. Olympia served as the territorial capital since 1853 and was a contender in the statewide election to name a state capital in 1889. The city received more votes than its challengers, North Yakima and Ellensburg, and defeated them in a subsequent runoff election, per the Washington Secretary of State . WEST VIRGINIA: Charleston Charleston, West Virginia. 6381380/Getty Images/iStockphoto Charleston only became West Virginia's permanent capital after a lengthy feud with another city, Wheeling. From 1863 to 1885, the capital alternated between the two cities three times, with critics of Wheeling arguing it wasn't as centrally located as Charleston. Charleston was ultimately decided the winner in an 1877 election, becoming the permanent capital eight years later, per the West Virginia Encyclopedia Online . WISCONSIN: Madison Madison, Wisconsin. John Touscany/Getty Images When Wisconsin was a territory, Belmont briefly served as its original capital. Legislators quickly sought a new capital city, and the politician and land speculator James Duane Doty proposed his empty plot of land, Wisconsin Public Radio reported . Doty lobbied legislators with real-estate opportunities and even robes, and Madison was made the new capital in an ensuing legislative vote. WYOMING: Cheyenne Cheyenne, Wyoming. Cheri Alguire/Getty Images Cheyenne's founding coincided with the Union Pacific Railroad's westward expansion. The company planned to develop a townsite in the area, and Cheyenne was settled in 1867, becoming the capital of the Wyoming Territory two years later, per WyoHistory.org . The city remained the capital after Wyoming was granted statehood in 1890. Read the original article on Business Insider

Today, in 17 states, the capital is also the most populous city. Phoenix, the nation's most populous state capital, has more than 1.6 million residents, while Montpelier, Vermont, has fewer than 8,000, according to the latest Census estimates.

But population was often far from the deciding factor when designating a state capital. Many were selected hundreds of years ago, when some of today's cities were little more than stretches of undeveloped land.

Some were simply designated as state capitals by legislative or popular vote, while others were subject to political trickery and corruption, and some were chosen because they were the sites of new, booming industries. In a few cases, townspeople even chipped in to fund the new capitol buildings.

Most commonly, cities were chosen based on their geographic location. Before modern transportation, rivers and railroads were the best means of transit. As such, many state capitals sit along rivers or were chosen for their central locations to allow legislators to travel easily from every corner of the state.

From Alabama to Wyoming, see how every state's capital earned the title.

ALABAMA: Montgomery
Montgomery, Alabama.

fotoguy22/Getty Images

Though Alabama became a state in 1819, Montgomery didn't become its capital until 1846. Before statehood, the territorial capital was located in the town of St. Stephens, chosen for its proximity to the Tombigbee River, according to the Montgomery Advertiser.

The capital soon changed to Huntsville, then Cahaba and Tuscaloosa, after statehood. Montgomery was finally decided upon for its central location amid changes in the state's transportation, economy, and geography, the Advertiser reported.

ALASKA: Juneau
Juneau, Alaska.

JillianCain/Getty Images

Anchorage is Alaska's most populous city with nearly 300,000 residents, per the most recent Census estimates. But Alaska's capital sits more than 500 miles southeast in the small city of Juneau.

Juneau's initial growth came in part from its booming gold-mining industry. When it became the new capital of territorial Alaska in 1906, it was Alaska's biggest city, according to KTOO. The capital city was previously Sitka, which sits on an island in Alaska's Alexander Archipelago.

In Juneau's 120-year history as Alaska's capital, many efforts in the state legislature have been made to move the capital to Anchorage, largely because of travel difficulties for elected officials.

In 1974, voters approved an initiative to relocate the capital, but subsequent proposals to finance the move were rejected, KTOO reported.

ARIZONA: Phoenix
Phoenix, Arizona.

Leonid Andronov/Getty Images

Arizona's territorial capital moved from Prescott to Tucson, back to Prescott, and finally to Phoenix in 1889, per KJZZ Phoenix.

Phoenix, originally founded as Swilling's Mill in 1867 by a Confederate veteran, started to expand toward the end of the 19th century. It was chosen as the capital in 1889 due to its growing significance in transportation and agriculture. It wasn't until 1912 that Arizona became a state.

Today, Phoenix is home to 1.67 million residents and is the most populous state capital in the US.

ARKANSAS: Little Rock
Little Rock, Arkansas.

ChrisBoswell/Getty Images/iStockphoto

When Arkansas was a territory, its capital sat in Arkansas Post, a location which held significance during French and Spanish control of the area, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas. However, it was also the site of flooding and illnesses like malaria.

Little Rock was chosen as the territory's capital in 1821 largely due to interest from settlers. Located along the Arkansas River, the new settlement allowed for travel via the Mississippi River. Arkansas was granted statehood 15 years later.

CALIFORNIA: Sacramento
Sacramento, California.

casch/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Though Monterey served as California's capital during Spanish and Mexican rule, San Jose was the first designated capital when California became a US state, per the California Capitol Museum.

The capital moved to Vallejo before Sacramento was chosen for its proximity to rivers, as well as the infrastructure and transportation links it already had in place.

Just two months after moving its headquarters to Sacramento, the state government was forced to move back to Vallejo due to flooding. The capital later moved to Benicia before permanently returning to Sacramento.

COLORADO: Denver
Denver, Colorado.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images

Before Colorado was a state, Colorado City and Golden served as its capital cities in the 1860s. Denver, becoming a growing population center and commercial hub, was picked as the temporary capital in 1876.

In 1881, voters chose to keep Denver as the capital in a referendum, according to the Colorado State Capitol Visitor Guide.

CONNECTICUT: Hartford
Hartford, Connecticut.

ChrisBoswell/Getty Images

Connecticut's capital history dates back to the turn of the 18th century. In 1701, the Connecticut Colony's General Court established two capital cities: Hartford and New Haven. General Assembly meetings would alternate between the two locations, according to Connecticut History.

In the 1870s, the state held a referendum to choose between the two cities, citing the impracticality of the current system. Hartford won out and officially became the state's capital in 1875.

DELAWARE: Dover
Dover, Delaware.

hyderabadi/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Delaware's capital came about as a direct result of the Revolutionary War. As the British moved to seize territory in Delaware in 1777, the capital of New Castle was moved to Dover over safety concerns and for its strategic central location, per Delaware Historical & Cultural Affairs.

FLORIDA: Tallahassee
Tallahassee, Florida.

Aneese/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Like Connecticut, Florida originally had two capitals. When it first became a US territory, lawmakers would alternate between St. Augustine and Pensacola, which are nearly 400 miles apart. Travel was dangerous and would take weeks, according to the Florida Department of State.

Legislators decided to meet in the middle for Florida's new capital. They chose Tallahassee, the midway point between the two cities, in 1824.

GEORGIA: Atlanta
Atlanta, Georgia.

felixmizioznikov/Getty Images

Before Atlanta was chosen as Georgia's capital in the 1870s, a handful of other cities had held the designation. Savannah, Augusta, Louisville, and Milledgeville were all Georgia's capital at one point, with the latter holding the title for 60 years, according to the New Georgia Encyclopedia.

Atlanta was ultimately chosen because of its significance as a railroad hub.

HAWAII: Honolulu
Honolulu, Hawaii.

mj0007/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Honolulu's status as Hawaii's capital dates to half a century before the islands were annexed by the US. In 1845, Hawaii's monarch, King Kamehameha III, moved the royal buildings from Lahaina, on the island of Maui, to Honolulu due to its harbor and growing commerce, and its easier access for visiting dignitaries.

After the government was overthrown in 1893, the provisional government and then the Republic of Hawaii continued to operate out of the city, per the National Park Service. It remained the capital after Hawaii became a state in 1959.

IDAHO: Boise
Boise, Idaho.

Seibel Photography LLC/Getty Images/iStockphoto

When Idaho was established as a US territory in 1863, Lewiston initially served as its capital. This was soon changed to Boise because of a population and mining boom in the city.

When the change was made, soldiers forcefully entered the capitol building in Lewiston and transported the territorial seal and papers to Boise. Today, some residents of Lewiston still believe their city's status as the capital was "stolen," the Idaho Press reported.

ILLINOIS: Springfield
Springfield, Illinois.

Sean Pavone/Getty Images

Illinois' original capital was Kaskaskia, located along the Mississippi River. Vandalia then served as the capital for two decades before an effort in the state legislature led by a young Abraham Lincoln resulted in Springfield being named the capital, according to the Illinois Secretary of State.

The gradual move northward reflected a growing population in the northern half of the state.

INDIANA: Indianapolis
Indianapolis, Indiana.

RudyBalasko/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Corydon was Indiana's original capital when it was a territory and during its early years of statehood. In the 1820s, Indianapolis was established as the state's new capital for its central location, per the Indiana Historical Society.

IOWA: Des Moines
Des Moines, Iowa.

Jacob Boomsma/Getty Images/iStockphoto

When Iowa became a territory in 1838, Burlington served as its capital, and it was soon replaced by Iowa City. However, legislators quickly desired a more central location for the capital, according to Iowa PBS.

Fort Des Moines, as it was known at the time, was chosen because it sat within 2 miles of the intersection of the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers.

KANSAS: Topeka
Topeka, Kansas.

MattGush/Getty Images

During the state's territorial struggle over slavery, Lecompton, Leavenworth, Pawnee, and present-day Fairway all spent time as the capital of Kansas for different governments, in addition to Lawrence serving as the then-territory's de facto capital from 1858 to 1861, the Topeka Capital-Journal reported.

Topeka was first chosen as the temporary capital in 1859, and it was made permanent in an election-day vote two years later, per the Kansas Historical Society.

KENTUCKY: Frankfort
Frankfort, Kentucky.

Sean Pavone/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Since Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort has served as the Bluegrass State's capital. While different cities vied for capital status, Frankfort won in part because its supporters offered gold and even a log cabin to the commissioners overseeing the decision, per the Kentucky Historical Society.

LOUISIANA: Baton Rouge
Baton Rouge, Lousiana.

CRobertson/Getty Images

Baton Rouge sits as Louisiana's capital because of a deliberate effort to shift power away from New Orleans, according to the museum Louisiana's Old State Capitol. Per the museum, in 1845, "a new state constitution mandated the location be 'not less than 60 miles from the city of New Orleans.'" Baton Rouge sits along the Mississippi River, roughly 80 miles northeast of New Orleans.

From 1829 to 1831, Donaldsonville briefly served as the state's capital, according to the city.

MAINE: Augusta
Augusta, Maine.

HABesen/Getty Images

Maine's capital was originally Portland, currently the state's largest city. However, the city's coastal location was the cause of concern in the 1820s, with some worrying it was vulnerable to attack, News Center Maine reported.

Maine's legislature sought a more central location in the state, eventually choosing Augusta, partly because the city offered to pay for construction of a capitol building.

MARYLAND: Annapolis
Annapolis, Maryland.

Amy Sparwasser/Getty Images

In colonial times, Maryland's capital was the town of St. Mary's City, located near the base of the Potomac River. Near the end of the 17th century, the colony's general assembly moved the capital to Anne Arundel Town — now known as Annapolis — due to population growth in the northern part of the colony, according to Maryland State Archives.

MASSACHUSETTS: Boston
Boston, Massachusetts.

ChrisBoswell/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Boston is one of the oldest capitals in the US, holding the title in Massachusetts for nearly 400 years. The city was designated as the capital of the Massachusetts Bay Colony when Puritan settlers, led by John Winthrop, established it in the 1630s.

Winthrop first settled in Salem before moving to Boston, according to the Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth.

MICHIGAN: Lansing
Lansing, Michigan.

fotoguy22/Getty Images

Having originally served as Michigan's territorial capital, Detroit was chosen as Michigan's capital after statehood was granted in the 1830s. This was a temporary measure, however, with Michigan's constitution noting it would serve as the capital "until the year eighteen-hundred and forty-seven, when it shall be permanently located by the Legislature," according to the Michigan State Capitol.

The empty space that would later become Lansing was chosen, even though people at the time called it a "howling wilderness," according to the Capitol. Legislators met in a temporary wooden building before the town was constructed, and it wasn't until 1859 that it was incorporated as a city.

Lansing was chosen for its central location, according to Downtown Lansing Inc.

MINNESOTA: St. Paul
Saint Paul, Minnesota.

AndreyKrav/Getty Images/iStockphoto

St. Paul has served as Minnesota's capital since it became a US territory in 1849, according to the Minnesota Historical Society. It was likely chosen for its location along the Mississippi River and the area's population growth.

In 1857, a bill in Minnesota's territorial legislature threatened to move the capital to St. Peter. Legislator Joseph Rolette, once he was in possession of the bill, intentionally went missing to prevent its passage. While Rolette is often credited with preventing the move from taking place, the incident was largely symbolic as the bill also failed to pass on legal grounds, per the Minnesota Historical Society.

MISSISSIPPI: Jackson
Jackson, Mississippi.

SeanPavonePhoto/Getty Images/iStockphoto

The towns of Natchez, Washington, and Columbia all at one point served as the capital of Mississippi when it was a territory and in its early statehood, the Clarion-Ledger reported. Like other states, however, legislators sought a more central location for the capital.

The location that became Jackson was chosen because it sat at the intersection of trade routes, per Mississippi History Now. Incorporated in 1822, the city was named after Andrew Jackson.

MISSOURI: Jefferson City
Jefferson City, Missouri.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images

St. Louis originally served as the capital of the Missouri territory before St. Charles was named the temporary capital when Missouri became a state in 1821.

Jefferson City, then an undeveloped site, was picked as "a compromise between two major population centers," according to the city. It has served as Missouri's capital since 1826.

MONTANA: Helena
Helena, Montana.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images

The capital of Montana was set to be decided by voters in the election of 1892. Seven cities competed, and while the election didn't produce a winner, it left Anaconda and Helena as the clear frontrunners, according to Visit Southwest Montana.

People in both cities campaigned for the capital, with a winner to be decided in the election of 1894. Helena was victorious, winning by a margin of just 1.8% — fewer than 2,000 votes.

NEBRASKA: Lincoln
Lincoln, Nebraska.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images

While Omaha had served as Nebraska's capital when it was a territory, many Nebraskans wanted a change, according to the Nebraska State Historical Society.

A new site — named Lincoln after the recently assassinated president — was chosen southwest of Omaha, in part because it was south of Nebraska's Platte River, which was difficult to cross at the time, and most of the population lived south of the river.

NEVADA: Carson City
Carson City, Nevada,

pabradyphoto/Getty Images

Carson City has always served as Nevada's capital. The city was settled as a proper community in 1858. In 1859, the area saw a commercial boom after gold and silver were discovered nearby, per Visit Carson City.

In 1861, it was named the territorial capital, and it remained the capital when Nevada became a state in 1864.

NEW HAMPSHIRE: Concord
Concord, New Hampshire.

Sanghwan Kim/Getty Images

Before Concord, other cities, such as Exeter, served as New Hampshire's capital, according to the Exeter Historical Society.

Concord became the capital in 1808 for its central location, according to the city.

NEW JERSEY: Trenton
Trenton, New Jersey.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images

Like many other state capitals, Trenton was chosen as New Jersey's capital city in 1790 largely due to geographic factors.

The city is located between New York City and Philadelphia and sits along the Delaware River, which was significant for trade and transportation, per Trenton Daily.

NEW MEXICO: Santa Fe
Santa Fe, New Mexico.

4nadia/Getty Images

Spanish colonists established Santa Fe as the capital of Nuevo México in 1610. It then continued to serve as the capital of the province under Mexican rule, and later the capital of the US territory and state, according to Tourism Santa Fe.

NEW YORK: Albany
Albany, New York.

BRULIN REMI/Getty Images

While Kingston briefly served as New York's first capital, the city was burned down by the British during the Revolutionary War.

Albany, farther up the Hudson River, held significance during the war for its role in military planning and the distribution of supplies. For these reasons, Albany was named New York's capital in 1797, News 10 New York reported.

NORTH CAROLINA: Raleigh
Raleigh, North Carolina.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images

The cities of Bath, Edenton, and New Bern all served as the capital of North Carolina before Raleigh was chosen. The latter, then just a grove of trees, was ultimately selected as the permanent capital in 1792 because of its central location, North Carolina's Our State Magazine reported.

NORTH DAKOTA: Bismarck
Bismarck, North Dakota.

4nadia/Getty Images/iStockphoto

When North and South Dakota were unified as the Dakota Territory, Yankton — now in South Dakota — originally served as its capital. However, many Dakotans thought it was too far away from the growing cities of Deadwood and Fargo. Additionally, Yankton didn't sit along a transcontinental railroad line, according to North Dakota Studies.

In the 1880s, a commission was appointed to locate a new suitable capital for the territory. The process was plagued by corruption, including members of the commission being given financial incentives to vote for Bismarck. The northern city won and remained the capital of North Dakota when the Dakotas were admitted to the Union as separate states.

OHIO: Columbus
Columbus, Ohio.

Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Chillicothe served as Ohio's original capital when statehood was granted, and Zanesville later acted as the state's temporary capital.

However, a piece of legislation in 1810 ordered that a permanent capital must be "not more than 40 miles from what may be deemed the common center of the state," according to the Ohio Statehouse. This meant a new capital was to be chosen.

The site that would become Columbus was picked in 1812 for its central location.

OKLAHOMA: Oklahoma City
Oklahoma City, Oklahoma.

benkrut/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Guthrie originally served as Oklahoma's territorial capital and later its state capital. However, Oklahoma City was seeing rapid growth and became the state's leading population center, prompting a statewide vote to make the city Oklahoma's capital.

The vote was successful, and Oklahoma City became the capital in 1910, according to the Oklahoma Historical Society.

OREGON: Salem
Salem, Oregon.

4nadia/Getty Images/iStockphoto

When Oregon was a territory, Oregon City initially served as its capital. Salem took over as capital in 1851, and, as a compromise, other cities, such as Portland, were given other public institutions, according to the Willamette Heritage Center.

Even after Salem remained the capital when Oregon achieved statehood, many citizens and legislators were unhappy with the choice. Following a wave of legal challenges and efforts to move the capital elsewhere, elections in 1862 and 1864 finalized the city as the state's capital.

PENNSYLVANIA: Harrisburg
Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

Mak Studio/Getty Images

William Penn originally chose Philadelphia as the capital of Pennsylvania in the 17th century, a status it held until 1799. During the Revolutionary War, the Second Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence in the state house, now known as Independence Hall, according to the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission.

The capital was moved west to Lancaster, and later to Harrisburg in 1812, for lawmakers to convene in a more central location.

RHODE ISLAND: Providence
Providence, Rhode Island.

Ray Tan/Getty Images

Like other states, Rhode Island had multiple capitals. Legislators alternated between county state houses in five different towns — Providence, Newport, Bristol, East Greenwich, and Kingston — for sessions until 1854, when it was narrowed down to Newport and Providence, according to Newport History.

As Providence's influence grew, it was named the state's sole capital in 1900.

SOUTH CAROLINA: Columbia
Columbia, South Carolina.

Kruck20/Getty Images

Charleston originally served as South Carolina's capital, but a 1786 assembly vote changed it to Columbia. The city's central location made it a more desirable capital than coastal Charleston, according to the South Carolina Statehouse.

SOUTH DAKOTA: Pierre
Pierre, South Dakota.

Gabriel Shakour/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Even though Yankton, the original capital of the Dakota Territory, was located in the new state of South Dakota, it was never considered for the capital when the state was admitted into the Union in 1889.

Pierre, which is in the middle of the state and located on the Missouri River, was chosen as a temporary capital that year, Dakota News Now reported.

It remained as the capital after it received the most votes in an 1890 statewide election.

TENNESSEE: Nashville
Nashville, Tennessee.

Nicholas Klein/Getty Images

After Tennessee became a state, Knoxville, Kingston, Nashville, and Murfreesboro all served as its capital at one point. It wasn't until an 1843 Tennessee General Assembly vote that Nashville was named the permanent capital.

The decision was likely due to the city's commercial and cultural status, as well as its central location in the state, according to Nashville Adventures.

TEXAS: Austin
Austin, Texas.

CrackerClips/Getty Images/iStockphoto

The area that became Texas had different capitals at different times under Spanish and Mexican rule. When Texas was an independent republic from 1836 to 1846, it also had several capitals, most notably Houston and Austin.

The latter — originally called Waterloo — remained the capital when Texas was annexed by the US, per the Texas Almanac.

UTAH: Salt Lake City
Salt Lake City, Utah.

miroslav_1/Getty Images/iStockphoto

When Utah was a territory, a small town in the middle of the state called Fillmore — named after the 13th US president — was designated as the capital.

However, the town's expected growth never materialized, and the more populous and commercially successful Salt Lake City was designated as the territory's new capital in the 1850s, per the Utah History Encyclopedia.

VERMONT: Montpelier
Montpelier, Vermont.

4nadia/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Vermont didn't have a proper capital until the 19th century, when Montpelier was chosen in 1805, the Vermont Daily Chronicle reported. Before then, legislators would alternate between 14 different locations.

Montpelier was decided upon because of its central location, as well as the town's citizens personally raising funds to build the capitol.

VIRGINIA: Richmond
Richmond, Virginia.

eurobanks/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Jamestown served as the original capital of the Colony of Virginia for most of the 17th century, before the capital was moved to Williamsburg in 1699, according to the Virginia General Assembly.

During the Revolutionary War, Thomas Jefferson, then the governor of Virginia, led an effort to move the capital to Richmond, and it officially became the capital in 1780.

Supporters cited it as safer than Williamsburg from a potential British attack while still sitting along a river (although British forces would attack the city in 1781) and more centrally located for the state's growing population.

WASHINGTON: Olympia
Olympia, Washington.

ChrisBoswell/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Olympia's status as Washington's capital dates back to when the Evergreen State was still a territory. Olympia served as the territorial capital since 1853 and was a contender in the statewide election to name a state capital in 1889.

The city received more votes than its challengers, North Yakima and Ellensburg, and defeated them in a subsequent runoff election, per the Washington Secretary of State.

WEST VIRGINIA: Charleston
Charleston, West Virginia.

6381380/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Charleston only became West Virginia's permanent capital after a lengthy feud with another city, Wheeling. From 1863 to 1885, the capital alternated between the two cities three times, with critics of Wheeling arguing it wasn't as centrally located as Charleston.

Charleston was ultimately decided the winner in an 1877 election, becoming the permanent capital eight years later, per the West Virginia Encyclopedia Online.

WISCONSIN: Madison
Madison, Wisconsin.

John Touscany/Getty Images

When Wisconsin was a territory, Belmont briefly served as its original capital. Legislators quickly sought a new capital city, and the politician and land speculator James Duane Doty proposed his empty plot of land, Wisconsin Public Radio reported.

Doty lobbied legislators with real-estate opportunities and even robes, and Madison was made the new capital in an ensuing legislative vote.

WYOMING: Cheyenne
Cheyenne, Wyoming.

Cheri Alguire/Getty Images

Cheyenne's founding coincided with the Union Pacific Railroad's westward expansion. The company planned to develop a townsite in the area, and Cheyenne was settled in 1867, becoming the capital of the Wyoming Territory two years later, per WyoHistory.org.

The city remained the capital after Wyoming was granted statehood in 1890.

items.summary: The Washington Post's opinion editor is leaving after about a year. Kevin Carter/Getty Images The Washington Post's opinion editor said he's decided to leave after about a year. Adam O'Neal was hired as part of a shake-up pushed by owner Jeff Bezos. O'Neal said under him, the opinion page became "more relevant, accessible, and consequential." The Washington Post's opinion editor is leaving after about a year. Adam O'Neal was hired as part of owner Jeff Bezos's push to champion "personal liberties and free markets" in the opinion section. O'Neal had been a correspondent at The Economist. A replacement hasn't been named. Bezos unveiled the changes to the Post's opinion page in a note to staff in early 2025. "We are going to be writing every day in support and defense of two pillars: personal liberties and free markets," Bezos wrote at the time . "We'll cover other topics too of course, but viewpoints opposing those pillars will be left to be published by others." While newspaper owners generally set the direction of opinion pages, the shake-up sparked criticism. Former Post editor Martin Baron said it ran counter to the paper's history of championing editorial independence. "Bezos argues for personal liberties," Baron said at the time. "But his news organization now will forbid views other than his own in its opinion section." In a Friday memo, O'Neal said that the section's work had "become more relevant, accessible, and consequential" during his tenure. "During my first six months, Opinions users more than doubled their time spent on the site," he wrote. "Editorial pageviews grew by triple-digits year over year." "Both subscription starts and entrances from search ticked up," he added. Below are the memos that O'Neal and acting publisher and CEO Jeff D'Onofrio sent on Friday: Here's O'Neal's memo: Team, I'm writing to announce that I have decided to leave The Washington Post. My last day will be August 31. It has been a remarkable year, and I'm very proud of everything we've accomplished together. I joined The Post to lead the opinion section as it began a new chapter, and we have made dramatic changes over the past year. We quickly embraced our mission of championing free markets and personal liberties while simultaneously putting Post Opinions on a sustainable footing. Our work has become more relevant, accessible and consequential. We regularly publish world-class journalism that finds the audience where it is. This includes agenda-setting columns; news-breaking op-eds; highly influential editorials; and social media content that reaches millions of new people. During my first six months, Opinions users more than doubled their time spent on the site; editorial pageviews grew by triple-digits year over year; and both subscription starts and entrances from search ticked up. I want to thank Jeff Bezos, Jeff D'Onofrio and the entire leadership team. And I especially want to thank everyone in Post Opinions. It has been an honor to have worked with such exceptional people at such an exceptional institution. While this was not an easy decision, I am leaving proud of how far the opinion section has come and optimistic that its best days lie ahead. Please join me at 11:30 a.m. for an all-hands meeting. With gratitude, Adam D'Onofrio's memo: The Washington Post isn't The Washington Post without our Opinions section. Its critiques and columns spark robust discussion, and under the provenance of our owner, we opened the doors last year to a wider audience by examining today's issues under the lens of two values that are intrinsic to our country — free markets and personal liberties. This past year, under the leadership of Adam O'Neal, Post Opinions has become more balanced in perspective, more financially sustainable and more accessible to readers than ever before. As Adam shared, he has made the decision to step down, with Aug. 31 as his last day. I want to thank him for his leadership and hard work in reimagining the section. Over the coming weeks, we will work to transition Post Opinions leadership. More to come on that front. Jeff Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
The Washington Post's opinion editor is leaving after about a year.

Kevin Carter/Getty Images

  • The Washington Post's opinion editor said he's decided to leave after about a year.
  • Adam O'Neal was hired as part of a shake-up pushed by owner Jeff Bezos.
  • O'Neal said under him, the opinion page became "more relevant, accessible, and consequential."

The Washington Post's opinion editor is leaving after about a year.

Adam O'Neal was hired as part of owner Jeff Bezos's push to champion "personal liberties and free markets" in the opinion section. O'Neal had been a correspondent at The Economist. A replacement hasn't been named.

Bezos unveiled the changes to the Post's opinion page in a note to staff in early 2025.

"We are going to be writing every day in support and defense of two pillars: personal liberties and free markets," Bezos wrote at the time. "We'll cover other topics too of course, but viewpoints opposing those pillars will be left to be published by others."

While newspaper owners generally set the direction of opinion pages, the shake-up sparked criticism. Former Post editor Martin Baron said it ran counter to the paper's history of championing editorial independence.

"Bezos argues for personal liberties," Baron said at the time. "But his news organization now will forbid views other than his own in its opinion section."

In a Friday memo, O'Neal said that the section's work had "become more relevant, accessible, and consequential" during his tenure.

"During my first six months, Opinions users more than doubled their time spent on the site," he wrote. "Editorial pageviews grew by triple-digits year over year."

"Both subscription starts and entrances from search ticked up," he added.

Below are the memos that O'Neal and acting publisher and CEO Jeff D'Onofrio sent on Friday:

Here's O'Neal's memo:

Team,I'm writing to announce that I have decided to leave The Washington Post. My last day will be August 31. It has been a remarkable year, and I'm very proud of everything we've accomplished together.I joined The Post to lead the opinion section as it began a new chapter, and we have made dramatic changes over the past year. We quickly embraced our mission of championing free markets and personal liberties while simultaneously putting Post Opinions on a sustainable footing.Our work has become more relevant, accessible and consequential. We regularly publish world-class journalism that finds the audience where it is. This includes agenda-setting columns; news-breaking op-eds; highly influential editorials; and social media content that reaches millions of new people.During my first six months, Opinions users more than doubled their time spent on the site; editorial pageviews grew by triple-digits year over year; and both subscription starts and entrances from search ticked up.I want to thank Jeff Bezos, Jeff D'Onofrio and the entire leadership team. And I especially want to thank everyone in Post Opinions. It has been an honor to have worked with such exceptional people at such an exceptional institution.While this was not an easy decision, I am leaving proud of how far the opinion section has come and optimistic that its best days lie ahead. Please join me at 11:30 a.m. for an all-hands meeting.With gratitude,Adam

D'Onofrio's memo:

The Washington Post isn't The Washington Post without our Opinions section. Its critiques and columns spark robust discussion, and under the provenance of our owner, we opened the doors last year to a wider audience by examining today's issues under the lens of two values that are intrinsic to our country — free markets and personal liberties.This past year, under the leadership of Adam O'Neal, Post Opinions has become more balanced in perspective, more financially sustainable and more accessible to readers than ever before.As Adam shared, he has made the decision to step down, with Aug. 31 as his last day. items.title: We Are Alarmed by This PR Firm Using a Small Army of Fake AI-Powered Publicists to Barrage Journalists With Pitches for Its Clients
items.summary: Does it ever feel like your inbox is filling up with emails that don’t sound quite human? You may be right. Last week, I received an email from a publicist identified as “June Barton,” whose address indicated that she worked at a firm called VectorGuideHQ. The message, which read like any one of the countless PR emails in my inbox, was seeking coverage for a wellness app called RiseGuide. Barton offered to set me up with an account and introduce me to the startup’s founder. When I didn’t respond, Barton followed up. “Glad to set you up so you can try it, or put you on a call with the founder,” Barton wrote. “Lmk!” RiseGuide is a real company. But June Barton is not a real PR rep, or even a real person. For one thing, her headshot — showing a light-eyed, soft-smiling brunette — was clearly AI-generated. Though not visible in the tiny email window, when I opened her profile picture in a new tab, I could see that the image had failed to cut out a watermark disclosing that it was downloaded from the site “this-person-does-not-exist.com,” which traffics in AI-generated faces. “Generate random human face in 1 click and download it!” reads this-person-does-not-exist.com. “AI generated fake person photos: man, woman or child.” Even more peculiar was that when I looked up the VectorGuideHQ site in Barton’s email address — june@vectorguidehq.com — it redirected to a United Kingdom-based PR company called Movchan Agency. Barton, I soon learned, was one character among a roster of fake personas used by Movchan to pitch journalists on stories. When I reached out to the firm’s clients, they said they were unaware of the practice. “We do work with Movchan Agency, but were not aware of these practices,” RiseGuide’s founder, Oleksandr Matsiuk, told me. “They are meant to act as our PR support and represent our brand by helping us with reaching out to reporters like yourself. Each story gets either created, or previously approved by us, however, we were not aware they were using AI-generated personas in the outreach process — otherwise we would’ve been naturally against it.” Searching my inbox, I realized that I’d been pitched by a small army of similar fake accounts operated by Movchan. For instance, earlier this week I got an email from a sender identified as “Summer Casey,” hailing from the address summer@lorvotieio.com. As with Barton’s message, the email, which was sent to pitch a company called AGI Inc, read like any other PR message for an AI company, promising that it would free up time for parents to spend more time with their children. But again, something about Casey’s headshot seemed off. Sure enough, when I inspected the image, it also had a watermark noting that it came from “this-person-does-not-exist.com.” And also like Barton, plugging her alleged employer’s website — lorvotieio.com — into my browser, I was redirected to the homepage of Movchan. Movchan, which represents a roster of tech clients and, according to its LinkedIn , specializes in “viral PR,” wasn’t mentioned anywhere in either of the emails. I started sifting through my inbox. All told, I found dozens of emails from at least fifteen distinct fake personas operated by Movchan, hailing from a potpourri of fake PR firms. There was “Abigail Anderson,” for instance, reaching out from “abigail@kirometaco.com,” as well as “Sarai Singleton” at “sarai@maviosharehq.com,” and “Scarlet Walton” at “scarlet@divojoinio.com.” Though their headshots didn’t come with the giveaway “this-person-does-not-exist.com” watermark, the images appeared decidedly machine-generated. None of these alleged PR reps had any online presence beyond of my personal inbox — which was strange, given their apparent careers as professional connectors. And just like Casey, each of these three new personas, who allegedly worked for different firms, had been pitching me on AGI Inc. And when I plugged each of the fake firms’ sites into my search bar, I was once again sent to Movchan’s site. Some of these characters, as in the cases of Barton, Casey, Anderson, Singleton, and Walton, weren’t presented as having any connection to Movchan. But other made-up reps were explicitly presented as real employees of the PR firm, albeit emailing from a range of different domains — like “Mia Wilson” at “mia@mvchnpr.design,” who signed off emails as a “PR Manager for Movchan Agency,” and “Natalie Hudson,” an alleged “PR Manager @ Movchan Agency” who sent emails from “natalie.hudson@movchanprboost.com.” Most of the fake personas I found, including Wilson and Hudson, weren’t equipped with profile pictures, rendering them them exceedingly more difficult to spot. And this was all just in my inbox. I couldn’t help but wonder how many other journalists were being pitched by fake personas operated by Movchan. If it’s happened to you, feel free to reach out to maggie@futurism.com . Several of Movchan’s clients said they had no idea the firm was operating fake characters on their behalf. “I had no idea they were using fake personas — this goes entirely against our brand values and standards. We are taking immediate action to put a stop to this right now,” said a representative for Joi AI, a startup that offers AI-powered romantic partners for people tired of a “frustrating dating app experience that leaves people feeling hurt, insecure, and alone.” Some of the story ideas that were pitched to me by phony Movchan representatives have wound up elsewhere in the news. In September, for instance, a fake persona named “Rosemary Dalton” sent me an email about a new survey from Joi AI. About a week after I received that email, the survey, as well as quotes from a Joi AI employee shared in that message, was included in coverage by The New York Post . According to LinkedIn, Movchan employs more than a dozen real human employees. So why was it emailing me with a rotation of fake ones? I reached out to company explaining what I’d found, and that its clients had told me they weren’t aware of the firm’s practice of using fake PR agents and firms. In response, the company’s founder Nadya Movchan confirmed that the 15 different names I’d pulled from my inbox were those of fabricated personas. According to her, the practice started “a few months ago,” and was meant to be “temporary.” “A few months ago (likely after one of Gmail’s deliverability updates), we had a major issue with our domain reputation,” Movchan told Futurism . “While we started working on the recovery, we decided to purchase pre-warmed domains, so as not to halt outreach, as a temporary measure. They came with pre-warmed mailboxes with set names and pictures from the vendor.” It’s worth noting that I’ve received emails from fake Movchan personas dating back as far as September 2025, which was almost a year ago. According to Movchan, use of made-up representatives is “definitely not” the agency’s “normal operating practice.” “Using these pre-warmed domains was definitely poor judgment on my end,” she added. Though the senders and accounts were fake, Movchan maintained that each of these mailboxes was “operated by real people, who crafted story angles, pitches and managed the outreach — all done by humans doing normal PR work.” To that end, one of the weirder emails I received — once again on behalf of AGI Inc — was from a sender allegedly named “Isabella Brown.” According to her email address, Brown worked for a company called LunarPostHQ. “Regards, Isabella,” the sender signed off the email. In a follow-up message sent from the same account, however, the sender signed off with a completely different name — that of an identifiably human Movchan employee. “That was a real member operating the account,” Movchan told me, “and signing the follow-up with her name out of habit.” Out of curiosity, I decided to run emails sent to me by fake Movchan reps through Pangram, a service that identifies AI-generated text. The results were mixed. The emails from Summer Casey and June Barton came back as 100 percent AI-generated; others were identified as 100 percent human, while others were deemed by Pangram to be a mix of human-written and AI-generated content. Movchan also confirmed that her agency’s clients were unaware of the practice and said they would wind the operation down. “This was our decision, and we handled it badly,” said Movchan, adding that “regardless of the reason, our operational struggles with the domain didn’t justify this approach. This is definitely not the quality of work that I live up to as a founder, and I will make sure this does not happen again.” If the internet is feeling less real than ever in the age of AI, it’s because it is. Onward into the uncanny valley we go, one June Barton and Summer Casey at a time. items.title: Google Earth’s New AI Lets Anyone Fabricate Completely Bullshit Satellite Images
items.summary: On Thursday, Google introduced a new AI feature into Google Earth which lets anyone fabricate all sorts of misleading or straight up inaccurate satellite imagery, from making it look like a specific place has suffered a drone strike to manifesting a nuclear plant in Iran. Usually, Google Earth is an exceptionally useful tool for open source intelligence (OSINT) analysts to digitally monitor areas of interest and see how they change over time, say, during a conflict or disaster. Now, Google Earth can easily be used as a tool for disinformation. 💡 Do you work at Google? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. In 404 Media’s tests, we were able to add skyscrapers to a rural area, added a “homeless encampment” to a part of Los Angeles where homelessness has become a major political issue, added a “bomb blast and crater” to an area of Los Angeles, and digitally created protesters outside Google's own corporate buildings. One of the tests by 404 Media. “Tonight I typed just one sentence into Google Earth and put refugees near the Mexican border. Then I planted a nuclear plant in Iran. Then I put a fatal crash on a street in Amsterdam. Google’s own satellite imagery underneath all three. What on earth is Google doing?” Henk van Ess, an OSINT researcher, wrote in a blog post on Thursday. The button now available in the web version of Google Earth lets a user type in a prompt while hovering over their desired location to create something new there. It is powered by Google’s Nano Banana model, according to a Google statement. A fake protest outside Google corporate buildings. “If you type the address of your workplace and then prompt it to ‘make it look like a drone attack happened here,’ it will create a damning image that looks very close to what we’ve seen in Ukraine, Russia, the Middle East, and other war-torn conflict zones,” Ben Heubl, another OSINT professional, wrote in a LinkedIn post . Obviously, this isn’t great for ensuring that screenshots from Google Earth are showing what anywhere on the planet actually looks like in reality. “It’s harrowing and horrific, and it will make verification work much more difficult, Heubl added. Another of the tests by 404 Media. Asked for comment, Google pointed 404 Media to a tweet the company posted on Thursday. “We take misinformation seriously – every image created with Nano Banana in Google Earth includes the SynthID digital watermark, so if someone is unsure about an image, they can ask the Gemini app or use Lens in Search to see if the image was AI-generated. In addition, we prevent image creation on harmful topics and are continually updating our protections,” it read. This of course ignores the very obvious fact that plenty of people do not bother to verify themselves if an image is real or not. People spreading misinformation also often don’t care about eventually getting caught; they can cause a massive amount of damage to a certain conversation very quickly before anyone calls them out for their bullshit. Heubl added, “Even if you can use detection tools to determine that an image was altered by Google, there are ways to override those indicators, no matter what people tell you. This is BAD.” Update: this piece has been updated to include a screenshot and description of a fake AI-generated image showing protesters outside Google corporate buildings.

items.title: Palantir CEO says Dario Amodei is not the 'caricature' that Americans might believe him to be
items.summary: Palantir CEO Alex Karp said that AI companies were "wildly unlikable." John Lamparski/Getty Images Palantir CEO Alex Karp said that AI tokens created a "weird kind of slop" that benefited unproductive people. AI companies need forward-deployed engineers "that aren't just masturbating and selling tokens," Karp said in an all-hands. Karp defended Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. "He's not the caricature that many people, most Americans, believe," he said. Alex Karp continue to drag the AI labs — while defending one of their leaders, Dario Amodei. The Palantir CEO spent July outlining his thesis for "sovereign AI." Firms should want to keep their data, he said; they shouldn't fork it over to a third-party like OpenAI or Anthropic. (You might remember that testy CNBC interview .) In an all-hands meeting , Karp continued to lay out his theory — and rip into his AI competitors. He called the companies "wildly unlikable." "They are actually unwilling to respond to any questions about: How do you build the models without ripping off someone's IP, migrating your alpha to your model, and then competing against them?" he said. "They do this over and over." As in previous interviews, Karp said that he was speaking for enterprises, not from his personal opinion. He didn't find the AI companies "unlikable," he said. "I've spent a lot of time with Dario," Karp said, referring to the Anthropic CEO . "He's not the caricature that many people, most Americans, believe." Tokens have been a sticking point for Karp. The unit of AI measurement determines how much companies pay for the technology. In June, he compared tokenmaxxing — or spending as much on AI as possible — to porn addiction . Once again, Karp took aim at tokens. He said that Palantir's customers were asking: "Why am I paying for tokens that lead to this weird kind of slop that only makes the least productive people happy?" Palantir popularized the "forward-deployed engineer" model, making it one of the hottest jobs in tech . Google and AWS have both invested in FDEs; OpenAI created a dedicated organization for them. Karp said in June that OpenAI ripped Palantir off (poorly). In the all-hands, he painted a graphic picture of the forward-deployed engineers, saying that AI companies needed "FDEs that aren't just masturbating and selling tokens." "That's what these are actually doing," Karp said. "They sell tokens." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.summary: by Aarti Laddha , Richard Diaz-Cool , Rishika Idnani , Venkatesh Selveraj Netflix supports a vast and evolving set of features and content types, ranging from 4K streaming and immersive audio to live streaming and cloud gaming, across a diverse ecosystem of devices. However, not all devices are created equal. Hardware limitations such as available RAM, CPU cores, display capabilities, or platform support mean that some features cannot be supported on certain device models. To ensure the best possible user experience, we rely on a deep understanding of device capabilities. We have invested in building a comprehensive device capability data model and integrating feature flags from internal systems, paving the way for smarter, more granular feature management across our global device landscape. This approach helps us identify bottlenecks in feature penetration and accelerates the pace of innovation. We have designed our data storage and modeling strategies to efficiently support analytics at scale. We use a cumulative table to process information about the device’s capabilities. This table is structured to efficiently capture the latest state of each device and its associated capabilities (like Screen resolutions, Video Profiles Supported, Surround Sound, RAM size etc) making it ideal for analytics and reporting use cases. { "Screen Height": ["720"], "Screen Width": ["1280"], "Video Profiles": [ "playready", "hevc", ], } For aggregate analytics, we leverage a histogram table that captures active device counts over the past 28 days, broken down by device model and software version. This table also records the number of devices supporting specific capabilities, enabling detailed distribution analysis. One use case for this histogram data is to analyze the distribution of external display capabilities attached to streaming sticks. For example, the histogram below shows that out of total X number of devices, all supported the HD profile (playready), while only 20% devices supported the UHD profile (hevc). { "Video Profiles": { "playready": 100%, # HD profile "hevc": 20% # UHD profile } } We have built analytical products that leverage these datasets to provide a comprehensive view of feature reach such as 4K Ultra HD, Netflix Spatial Audio, Cloud Gaming and the latest UI. By relying on data-driven insights, we can make informed decisions about which features to enable on specific devices, ensuring both performance and reliability. Modeling Device Capabilities for Analytics was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
